# kernl docs

> Developer documentation for kernl, an opinionated shell for sandboxed web applets built on the kehto toolkit.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/agent-access.md -->

# Agent access

How an AI agent should read these docs. This page describes website plumbing only; it is not part of any protocol.

## What is served

Everything below is relative to the docs root, `/docs/` by default. On the GitHub Pages deployment the root is `https://kernlize.github.io/docs/`.

| Want | Fetch |
| --- | --- |
| An index of every docs page, grouped like the sidebar, with one-line descriptions | `/docs/llms.txt` ([llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) format) |
| Every docs page in one file | `/docs/llms-full.txt` |
| One page as Markdown | The page path with `.md`: `/docs/index.md`, `/docs/concepts/guard.md`, `/docs/packages/index.md` |
| The generated API reference | `/docs/api/index.html` and `/docs/api/modules/_kernl_<package>.html`; HTML only |
| The landing site's own index | `/llms.txt` and `/llms-full.txt` at the site root, built by the Astro site |

## Markdown twins

Every HTML page on this docs site has a Markdown twin at a fixed path, generated at build time from the same source as the HTML:

- A page served at `/docs/concepts/guard` (or `/docs/concepts/guard.html`) has its twin at `/docs/concepts/guard.md`.
- A directory page such as `/docs/packages/` has its twin at `/docs/packages/index.md`.
- The docs root `/docs/` has its twin at `/docs/index.md`.

Each HTML page names its twin in `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="/docs/concepts/guard.md">
```

In the twins, frontmatter is removed, `:::` containers become blockquotes with a bold label, and internal links are rewritten to absolute `.md` URLs so a twin can be read on its own. Links into the generated API reference keep their `.html` extension because TypeDoc output has no Markdown form.

## Reading order

1. Fetch `/docs/llms.txt` and pick the section you need. The sections mirror the sidebar: Start, Concepts, Tutorials, How-tos, Packages, Reference, Policies.
2. For a question about behaviour, read the concept page first (for example `/docs/concepts/guard.md`), then the how-to.
3. For a question about an export, read the package page (`/docs/packages/<name>.md`) for the version, install line and export list, then the TypeDoc module page for signatures.
4. Treat `/docs/alpha-status.md` as authoritative about what is implemented. A contract described in a concept page may be an interface without a backend; the status page says which.

## What these docs are not

They are not the protocol. NIP-5D is specified in [nostr-protocol/nips PR #2303](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2303) and the NAP domains in [napplet/naps](https://github.com/napplet/naps). Where a kernl page and the specification disagree, the specification wins and the page has a bug; see [Spec conformance](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/spec-conformance.md).

They are also not the public website. The landing site at `/` follows the [public vocabulary](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/public-vocabulary.md) rule and never names a protocol. These pages name everything precisely because developers need the names.

## Build contract

`llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` and the twins are written by `docs/.vitepress/agent-output.ts` in VitePress's `buildEnd` hook. `scripts/audit-docs.mjs` fails the build when any of them is missing, so their presence is part of `pnpm docs:check`, not a convention.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md -->

# Alpha status

kernl is a first draft. This page says what runs, what is a contract without an implementation, and which upstream gaps are open. It is updated in the same pull request as the code it describes.

## What works

| Area | Package | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guard | `@kernl/guard` | Three profiles (`createGuardConfig`, `applyNappletRules`), envelope classification, ingress flood control with quarantine, visibility gate, focus-aware firewall over `@kehto/firewall`'s `evaluate()`, the fixed zero-network CSP, a port of kehto's unreleased nested-frame lock ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)), eleven mitigation descriptions for the UI. Pure, fully specified in `packages/guard/features/`. |
| Messaging | `@kernl/messaging` | `MessagingProvider`, `MessagingBackend`, `MessagingRegistry` with saved-preference restore, the composite backend with `provider:innerId` namespacing, `describeProvider` rows, a complete in-memory backend (`createMemoryBackend`) used by the preview and the tests, and three providers (`private`, `legacy`, `ratchet`) built with `defineProvider` from backends the shell injects. The network backends for `private` and `legacy` are in `@kernl/core` (`createPrivateMessagesBackend`, `createLegacyMessagesBackend`) and are wired in the live shell ([below](#messaging-providers-in-the-live-shell)). |
| Bridges | `@kernl/bridges` | `Locator` parsing for the web schemes, `magnet:`, `nzb:`, `slsk:` and `mailto:`, the `Bridge` contract, the registry with its `authorize` hook and outcome events, a complete HTTP bridge with SSRF policy, the four backend-driven bridges up to their backend interface, `createHandoffBackends`, which serves all four by opening the locator in an app on the user's device, `createBridgeResourceResolver` for kehto's resource service, and `describeBridge` rows. |
| Composition | `@kernl/core` | `createKernl` over one applesauce `EventStore`, `RelayPool` and `AccountManager`, with kehto's real `createShellBridge` exercised end to end in `kernl.feature`: an applet is decoded, resolved, planned and mounted, binds its port through the guarded `handleWindowMessage`, completes `shell.ready`, is answered by the theme, identity and resource services, and is quarantined and revoked when it floods. Relay tiers, the applesauce adapters, the guard pipeline and runtime firewall rules, grants over `bridge.runtime.aclState`, consent summaries, the default registries and the layouts each have their own feature file. |
| Shell UI | `apps/web` | Landing site at `/` and the shell at `/app/`: sign-in (browser extension, remote signer, read-only, password-protected local account), open by address with the required and optional domains as choices, windows, a grants panel per window, a shell-wide guard panel with the event log, the provider picker, and the offline preview behind `?preview=1` ([D-011](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-011)), hosted at [kernlize.github.io/app/?preview=1](https://kernlize.github.io/app/?preview=1). |

"Works" means the behaviour has a scenario in `packages/*/features/`, the scenario passes, and the page describing it exists. It does not mean the API is stable. Every package is `0.1.0`; on 0.x a breaking change is a minor bump.

## Messaging providers in the live shell

`createKernl` registers all three providers and, unless `KernlOptions.messagingBackends` overrides them, wires two real backends from `@kernl/core`: `createPrivateMessagesBackend` for `private` (NIP-17 gift-wrapped messages) and `createLegacyMessagesBackend` for `legacy` (NIP-04 direct messages). Both sign and encrypt with the active account's signer and nothing else ([D-015](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-015)). Availability follows the active account, and an unavailable provider reports a reason from `MESSAGING_UNAVAILABLE_REASONS`:

| Provider | Available when | Reason otherwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `private` | The active account's signer exposes `nip44` (browser extension, remote signer, password-protected local account) | `sign-in-required` with no active account; `signer-cannot-encrypt` when the signer has no `nip44` (a read-only account) |
| `legacy` | The active account's signer exposes `nip04` | `sign-in-required` with no active account; `signer-cannot-encrypt` when the signer has no `nip04` |
| `ratchet` | Never in this draft | `no-runtime`: a double-ratchet runtime has to be supplied |

`private` sends to the recipient's kind 10050 inbox relays, falling back to the sender's `outbox` and `super` tiers when the recipient publishes none, and wraps a copy to the sender so the conversation reads the same on every device. `legacy` is metadata-exposing: sender, recipient and timing are public on the event, and the picker says so. The Messages panel decrypts the user's own messages without a consent prompt, because the shell asks on the user's behalf; an applet reaches messages only through the `dm` domain grant. The preview still uses the in-memory backend.

## What does not work yet

- **In-shell transfer backends.** Downloads, sharing and mail work only by hand-off: `createKernl` passes `host.openLink` to `createDefaultBridges`, so the torrent, NZB, Soulseek and mail bridges open the locator's canonical address in an app on the user's device after the user confirms leaving kernl. kernl makes no connection for these; what the device app then does on its own network is outside kernl's view and control. No backend moves the data inside the shell, and there is no downloads view. A `job` result from a hand-off is an id, not a transfer kernl can track, and it is reported even when the user declines to leave. See [Bridges](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md#hand-off-backends).
- **Ratchet sessions.** No double-ratchet runtime ships, so `ratchet` reports `no-runtime` (the table above). See [Messaging](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/messaging.md).
- **Web fetch from the browser shell, beyond the simple case.** The HTTP bridge runs in the page, so it is subject to CORS, and an opaque redirect it cannot inspect is refused with `denied:redirect-unverifiable`. Web fetch works from the shell for `https` origins that permit cross-origin reads and answer without a redirect. Hostnames are checked as literals only; no resolver is wired. See [Bridges](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md#the-http-bridge).
- **Per-host bridge consent.** `createKernl` builds the bridge registry with `createDefaultBridges()` and no `authorize` hook, so a `resource` request from a granted applet is checked by the HTTP bridge's SSRF policy and nothing else. A host that wants a prompt per host or scheme passes its own registry in `KernlOptions.bridges`.
- **Per-applet guard profiles.** `GuardFacade.setProfile` rebuilds the pipeline for the whole shell and is not persisted. The per-applet, remembered override [D-003](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-003) describes is not in this draft.
- **Mobile layouts beyond the basics.** The layouts are desktop tilings over `@kehto/wm` ([Layouts](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/layouts.md)). At 720 px wide and below the shell switches to a compact layout: every window fills the desktop, and the bar keeps **Open** and moves the guard, messages, layout, minimised windows, settings and sign-out into a **Menu** sheet; panels open as full-width sheets. There are no gestures.
- **Multi-account switching.** `AccountManager` holds several accounts and the sign-in panel lists them, but switching means signing out and in.
- **Grant persistence across devices.** Grants, relay tiers and messaging preferences persist in the host's storage only. There is no sync. Every key is listed in [Persistence](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/persistence.md).
- **Packages on npm.** The `@kernl/*` packages are not published; they are used from a clone of the source repository, which is private during the alpha. See [Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install).
- **Source links in the API reference.** `typedoc.json` sets `packageOptions.disableSources: true`, so the generated reference has no "Defined in" source links. They would point at the source repository, which is private during the alpha.

The [Roadmap](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md) orders this list.

## Upstream gaps

kernl composes kehto rather than forking it ([D-001](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-001)). Four seams in kehto are narrower than kernl wants. All four are filed upstream against `kehto/web` rather than patched locally ([#397](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/397), [#398](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/398), [#399](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/399), [#400](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/400)). Each has a kernl layer that shrinks when it lands ([D-012](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-012)):

1. **`ShellAdapter` does not forward `getFocusContext`, `onFirewallEvent` or `firewallPersistence` to the runtime.** Without `getFocusContext` the runtime firewall treats every window as focused. kernl runs its focus-aware firewall in `@kernl/guard`, in front of the bridge for the window-level `hello` and as an observer of port traffic, using the pure `evaluate()` engine with visibility supplied by the host. Because that layer never supplies `initElapsedMs`, kehto's init-burst guard does not fire there, and the guard config's `burstGuard` is unused. The runtime does supply it, so the runtime's own startup burst guard (kehto's default, 20 operations in the first 3 s, `block`) refuses before dispatch. Without `onFirewallEvent` the runtime's refusals reach the applet as `firewall:` errors but not the host, so the guard panel shows kernl's own count of the same rates. ([kehto/web#397](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/397))
2. **`createRuntime` hardcodes the ACL default policy to `'permissive'`.** kernl produces its restrictive posture with `KernlGrants.ensure`, which writes an explicit grant or revoke for every capability of every applet it plans, plus `capabilities.resolveEnvironment`, which narrows the advertised domains to the baseline and the user's grants. The permissive default is never reached for an applet kernl runs. ([kehto/web#398](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/398))
3. **There is no hook that can hold or drop port traffic.** kehto calls `onNappletMessage` synchronously before it dispatches each envelope, but ignores its answer, so kernl's ingress guard, visibility gate and focus firewall can count and report an envelope but not refuse or delay it on their own. They have two effects. One is quarantine: revoking the binding inside the hook stops the envelope that crossed the limit, because kehto then finds no session for the window. Refusals come from the runtime's own firewall, configured through `applyRuntimeFirewallRules`. The other is the size cap, refused through that firewall: the runtime sizes only an envelope's `event`, so its matchers never see a download or a query, and kernl, which does measure them, sets the applet's runtime policy to `deny` for that one synchronous dispatch (`refuseCurrentDispatch`). Deferral while hidden is advisory for port traffic. See [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#where-enforcement-happens). ([kehto/web#399](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/399))
4. **The runtime firewall never applies an unfocused multiplier.** Because of gap 1 the runtime sees every window as focused, so its multiplier, whatever the value, never applies; and `FirewallStateContainer` has no setter for `unfocusedMultiplier`, so kernl could not install the profile's value even if focus were forwarded. The profile's value is applied only by kernl's focus firewall, which reports overruns rather than refusing them. ([kehto/web#400](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/400))

A fifth observation, not a gap kernl needs closed: the transport internals `createNip5dTransport` and `createShellReadyState` are not exported, so kernl uses `createShellBridge` unchanged.

One mitigation is carried locally rather than waiting upstream: `@kehto/shell` 0.29.0 leaves an applet free to create a child frame whose fresh realm still has WebRTC, and the lock that closes this exists only on kehto main behind `experimental.nestedContextLock`. `@kernl/guard` ports it and `planMount` always applies it, until a kehto release ships the flag ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)).

## Corrections

- **Rate enforcement (corrected 2026-11-03).** Earlier drafts of these docs, the README and D-012 said kehto's runtime firewall refused envelopes over the profile's rates. It did not: `applyRuntimeFirewallRules` also set each applet's runtime policy to `allow`, and kehto's `evaluate()` returns `pass` for an `allow` policy before it looks at any rate, matcher or burst. No rate was refused before dispatch; only kernl's reports and quarantine applied. The policy call is removed, the rates and kehto's startup burst guard now refuse before dispatch, and D-012 is rewritten to match.
- **Size caps (corrected 2026-11-03).** The guard's size matchers were described as able to report `matcher:size:<class>` in the shell. They cannot fire there: the ingress guard rejects the same envelopes first. Oversized downloads and queries were reported but still handled; they are now refused before dispatch.

## Versions this draft is built against

| Dependency | Range |
| --- | --- |
| `@kehto/acl` | `^0.20.2` |
| `@kehto/firewall` | `^0.6.3` |
| `@kehto/runtime` | `^0.27.2` |
| `@kehto/shell` | `^0.29.0` |
| `@kehto/services` | `^0.29.0` |
| `@kehto/nip` | `^0.8.0` |
| `@kehto/wm` | `^0.0.2` |
| `applesauce-*` | `^7.0.x` |
| `@napplet/core` | `>=0.37.0 <0.38.0` |

The protocol itself is a draft. NIP-5D is [nostr-protocol/nips PR #2303](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2303) and the NAP documents live at [napplet/naps](https://github.com/napplet/naps). kernl keeps no local copy of either; see [Spec conformance](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/spec-conformance.md).

# Changelog

Each entry says what ships, per package and app. [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md) is the current picture; this page is the history. Versions follow semver on 0.x: a breaking change is a minor bump.

## Unreleased

### `@kernl/core`

- `createPrivateMessagesBackend`: NIP-17 messages over the account signer. The seal is signed by the account with `nip44`; the wrap is signed by an ephemeral key that lives inside an applesauce `PrivateKeySigner` and is discarded after the wrap. Sends go to the recipient's kind 10050 inbox relays, falling back to the user's `outbox` and `super` tiers, with a copy wrapped to the user ([D-015](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-015)).
- `createLegacyMessagesBackend`: NIP-04 kind 4 messages through `signer.nip04`, normalised the same way and still marked metadata-exposing.
- `createKernl` wires both by default unless `KernlOptions.messagingBackends` overrides them, so `private` and `legacy` work in the live shell. Availability follows the active account: `private` needs a signer with `nip44`, `legacy` one with `nip04`.
- **Breaking.** `MESSAGING_UNAVAILABLE_REASONS` now holds `sign-in-required`, `signer-cannot-encrypt` and `no-runtime`. `needs-local-key-signer` and `not-implemented` are removed. See [Error reasons](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/reference/errors.md).

### Shell and site (`apps/web`)

- The Messages panel sends and receives private and legacy messages for an account whose signer can encrypt (browser extension, remote signer, password-protected local account). It opens the user's own messages without a consent prompt; applets still reach messages only through the `dm` grant.

## 0.1.0 — first draft, 2026-11-03

The first version of every package and of the shell. Nothing is published to npm yet; the packages are used from the source repository, which is private during the alpha ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)).

### `@kernl/guard` 0.1.0

- Three profiles, `strict`, `balanced` and `relaxed`, from `createGuardConfig`, and `applyNappletRules` for kehto's runtime firewall.
- Envelope classification, ingress flood control with quarantine, the visibility gate, and the focus-aware firewall over `@kehto/firewall`'s `evaluate()`.
- The fixed zero-network CSP from `createAppletCsp`, with the Trusted Types directives the frame lock needs.
- The nested-frame lock: a port of kehto's unreleased `experimental.nestedContextLock` ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)), described under Security below.
- Eleven mitigation descriptions for the guard panel. Pure; its one dependency is `@kehto/firewall`. See [`@kernl/guard`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/guard.md).

### `@kernl/messaging` 0.1.0

- The `MessagingProvider`, `MessagingBackend` and `MessagingRegistry` contracts, with saved-preference restore.
- The composite backend with `provider:innerId` namespacing, and `describeProvider` rows.
- A complete in-memory backend, `createMemoryBackend`, used by the preview and the tests.
- Three providers, `private`, `legacy` and `ratchet`, built with `defineProvider` from backends the host injects. No real backend ships, so all three are unavailable in the live shell. See [`@kernl/messaging`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/messaging.md).

### `@kernl/bridges` 0.1.0

- `parseLocator` for the web schemes, `magnet:`, `nzb:`, `slsk:` and `mailto:`, with `formatLocator` and `isNzbUrl`.
- The `Bridge` contract, the registry with its `authorize` hook and outcome events, and `describeBridge` rows.
- A complete HTTP bridge with an SSRF policy: `https` only, private and local destinations blocked, a byte limit on the streamed body, and opaque redirects refused in the browser.
- The torrent, NZB, Soulseek and mail bridges, and `createHandoffBackends`, which serves all four by opening the locator's canonical address in an app on the user's device ([Bridges](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md#hand-off-backends)).
- `createBridgeResourceResolver` for kehto's resource service. See [`@kernl/bridges`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/bridges.md).

### `@kernl/core` 0.1.0

- `createKernl`, the composition root: one applesauce `EventStore`, `RelayPool` and `AccountManager` over kehto's `createShellBridge`, exercised end to end in `kernl.feature`.
- Applet pointer decoding, manifest resolution, the mount plan and mounting.
- Grants over `bridge.runtime.aclState`, the restrictive environment resolver, and consent summaries for destructive writes.
- [Relay tiers](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/relay-tiers.md), [persistence](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/persistence.md) under the `kernl:` prefix with plaintext keys refused, the guard pipeline and runtime firewall rules, the default messaging and bridge registries, and four [layouts](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/layouts.md). See [`@kernl/core`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md).

### Shell and site (`apps/web`)

- The landing site at `/` and the shell at `/app/`.
- Sign-in with a browser extension, a remote signer, a read-only address or a password-protected local account.
- Open an applet by address, with its required and optional domains as choices.
- Floating and tiled windows, with a compact layout at 720 px and below.
- A grants panel per window, the shell-wide guard panel with its event log, the provider picker, and Settings for relay tiers.
- The offline preview behind `?preview=1` ([D-011](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-011)), hosted at [kernlize.github.io/app/?preview=1](https://kernlize.github.io/app/?preview=1).

### Docs

These pages, the TypeDoc API reference, `llms.txt` and a Markdown twin of every page, checked by `pnpm docs:check`: TypeDoc in strict mode, the docs audit, and every TypeScript sample compiled against the package sources.

### Security

The nested-frame lock ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)) closes a path an independent review found: applet code could create a child frame whose fresh realm still had a working `RTCPeerConnection`, which reached a public STUN server. `@kehto/shell` 0.29.0 removes the peer-connection globals from the applet's own realm only, and CSP does not govern WebRTC. The lock has three parts:

- **Static markup.** `assertAppletHasNoFrame` refuses frame, object and embed markup in the verified bytes with `denied:nested-frame` before they become a srcdoc.
- **Creation.** `renderFrameLockScript` installs a Trusted Types `default` policy that refuses frame markup at every HTML string sink, and pins the element factories so they refuse frame tag names. It runs before any applet script.
- **Insertion.** A second review found four creation routes past the factory pins. Because a frame only gets a realm once it is connected to the document, `appletInsertionLock` pins every DOM insertion method, including `Range.insertNode` and `Range.surroundContents`. It refuses any node that is, or contains, an HTML-namespace frame element. It reads node identity through native getters captured before applet code runs, refuses custom elements that extend frame elements, and removes `XSLTProcessor`.

`tests/e2e/applet-network-sealed.spec.ts` probes every route the reviews found, and thirteen insertion routes, and sees no child realm and no candidate. The cost: every DOM insertion in an applet walks the inserted subtree once.

### Corrections

Recorded in [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#corrections), both on 2026-11-03:

- **Rate enforcement.** Earlier drafts said kehto's runtime firewall refused envelopes over the profile's rates. It did not, because `applyRuntimeFirewallRules` also set each applet's runtime policy to `allow`, which passes before any rate is checked. The policy call is removed, the rates and kehto's startup burst guard now refuse before dispatch, and [D-012](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-012) is rewritten.
- **Size caps.** The guard's size matchers were described as able to fire in the shell. The ingress guard rejects the same envelopes first, so they could not. Oversized downloads and queries were reported but still handled; they are now refused before dispatch.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md -->

# Applets under kernl

kernl adds nothing to the applet format. An applet that conforms to NIP-5D and the NAPs runs in kernl. What kernl changes is the posture the applet meets: fewer domains until the user grants them, budgets the runtime enforces, no frames of its own, and a quarantine for applets that flood the shell. This page explains that posture from the applet's side and how to test against it.

## Use the applet SDK, not this repository

The applet side of the protocol is maintained at [napplet.run](https://napplet.run/docs/). Start there:

- [`@napplet/sdk`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@napplet/sdk) gives you typed named exports over `window.napplet` for bundler-based projects.
- [`@napplet/conformance`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@napplet/conformance) is the framework-agnostic conformance engine: a reference mock shell, per-NAP envelope validators, a manifest validator and reporters. `@napplet/conformance-cli` runs it from the command line.
- The [napplet.run getting-started guide](https://napplet.run/docs/guide/getting-started.html) and the [NAP documents](https://github.com/napplet/naps) are the authority on wire format and domain semantics.

kernl's packages are shell-side. You do not import them in an applet.

## What kernl advertises

`shell.init`, the shell's reply to your applet's `hello`, carries the domains this shell offers your applet's identity. In kernl that set is the shell's live domains narrowed by the user's grants (see [Identity and grants](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md)), so read it rather than assuming. The sets come from `BASELINE_DOMAINS` and `DOMAIN_CAPABILITIES` in `packages/core/src/grants/domain-capabilities.ts`, the services `createKernlServices` registers (`packages/core/src/kernl-services.ts`), and the domains kehto's runtime serves itself; [Architecture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md#where-each-nap-domain-is-served-from) has the same table from the shell's side.

| Posture | Domains | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline, advertised without a grant | `shell`, `inc`, `theme`, `storage` | `BASELINE_DOMAINS`. No network, and no account. Storage is the applet's own, read and write. A blocked applet sees `shell` alone. |
| Offered, advertised once the user grants it | `identity`, `relay`, `outbox`, `resource`, `dm`, `notify`, `link` | Backed by the services `createKernlServices` registers. `identity` is "your account" in the launcher: until it is granted, your applet is not told who is signed in. In the live shell `dm` reaches `private` and `legacy` while the signed-in account can encrypt; with nobody signed in no provider is available ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#messaging-providers-in-the-live-shell)). |
| Offered, advertised once granted, nothing wired behind it | `keys`, `media` | kehto's runtime serves these domains natively, so the shell offers them; kernl wires no host behaviour (hotkeys are not forwarded). |
| Not offered | `config`, `cvm`, `upload`, `intent`, `fs`, `llm`, `cache`, and every other domain | They have a row in `DOMAIN_CAPABILITIES` (or none), but no service is registered, so they are never advertised. |

Put a domain in `requires` only if your applet is useless without it. The launcher lists every domain you name in `requires` or `optional` as a switch that starts off on a first run, marks the required ones "the applet says it needs this", and warns when one is still off; the user can run your applet anyway, and then it sees the domain as unavailable. A user who switches on a domain this shell does not offer gets an error (`invalid:domain`) instead of your applet. Prefer `optional` and a graceful fallback.

## Where the guard acts on your traffic

kehto's bridge owns the port your applet talks over. kernl sees each envelope synchronously, just before kehto dispatches it, but cannot hold or drop it ([D-012](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-012)). Two layers follow from that, and they behave differently:

- **kehto's runtime firewall refuses.** It enforces the profile's per-class rates, which `kernl.mount` installs for your applet's `dTag`, and kehto's own startup burst guard. An over-budget envelope is refused by the runtime with an error that starts `firewall:`. kernl's size caps are refused the same way: kernl measures the envelope and has the runtime refuse that one dispatch.
- **kernl's guard reports, and quarantines.** It observes the same traffic with the shell's knowledge of visibility and focus and records guard events. Apart from the size caps it cannot refuse a single envelope, with one exception: when an envelope pushes your applet over a quarantine limit, kernl revokes the binding inside that observation, so that envelope is not dispatched and your applet is closed.

The window-level `hello` is the one message kernl filters before kehto sees it.

## What the strict profile means for you

The shell boots in `strict`. The numbers are in [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#profiles); the behaviours you will notice:

**Hidden windows are not paused.** While your window is minimised or the page is hidden, your envelopes are still dispatched; nothing is queued for later. The visibility gate holds only a window-level `hello` sent while hidden. What hiding changes is what kernl counts: hidden implies unfocused, so kernl's focus firewall measures you at the unfocused capacity and reports overruns, and resource requests count against the hidden allowance below, which does stop you. Still design as if delivery can stall: do not time out a request after a few seconds, and do not assume a subscription delivers while you are hidden. A true pre-dispatch hold is requested upstream ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#upstream-gaps)).

**Hidden resource allowance.** A hidden window may make 8 `resource.*` requests; the ninth quarantines it with `flood:hidden-resource`, and that ninth request is not dispatched. The count resets as soon as the window is visible again. Fetch what you need while visible.

**Rate limits by operation class.** Each class has its own token bucket, keyed by your applet's `dTag`, so two windows of your applet share one budget. In `strict`: 30 `relay.subscribe` and 20 `relay.publish` per minute, 20 `dm.send` and 10 `intent.*` per minute, 120 `resource.*` and 60 `storage.set`/`storage.remove` per 10 seconds. These are the limits the runtime enforces before dispatch, at full capacity whether or not your window is focused: kehto's `ShellAdapter` does not forward focus to the runtime, so its unfocused multiplier never applies. Deletions (kind 5) count against the `relay.publish` budget there and have no bucket of their own. kernl's focus firewall counts the same classes again, plus 5 deletions per minute, at 0.25 of capacity while your window is not focused, and reports each overrun as a guard event such as `rate:relay:publish` or `rate:relay:publish:delete`. Those reports do not refuse anything.

**Ingress flood control.** kernl counts 8 messages per second per window. Above that it reports `flood:burst` (and `flood:queue-full` once 64 are counted as waiting); for port traffic these are events only. The hard limit is real: the 300th message inside any rolling 10 seconds quarantines the window with `flood:quarantine`, and that message is not dispatched. Batch your writes and coalesce your subscriptions.

**Quarantine stops your applet.** A quarantined window has its binding revoked and its frame removed. The user sees "This applet was stopped." and can open your applet again in a fresh window; nothing resumes on its own.

**Envelope caps.** `resource.*` envelopes over 64 KiB and `relay.subscribe`/`outbox.subscribe` (including `outbox.query`) envelopes over 256 KiB are refused before dispatch: your applet receives a `firewall:` error, nothing is fetched, and the user sees a `size:<class>` guard event. Large filters are a smell; split them.

**A startup burst limit.** kehto's runtime counts every operation in your window's first 3 seconds and refuses everything past the 20th with a `firewall:` error. kernl also counts 8 messages per second from the first message, and reports bursts above that. Load lazily: request the first screen, render, then fetch the rest.

**No frames of your own.** kernl refuses to mount an applet whose markup contains an `iframe`, `frame`, `frameset`, `object`, `embed`, `portal` or `fencedframe` element (`denied:nested-frame`), and inside the window every way of creating one throws `TypeError: denied:nested-frame`: `createElement`, `createElementNS`, `createDocument`, and any HTML string with a frame tag written to `innerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write` or a parser. A child frame would be a fresh realm with a network path the shell cannot see ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)). Render into your own document instead. Two side effects to know: a string written to an HTML sink that merely mentions a frame tag, in text or an attribute, is refused too, so escape such text or set it with `textContent`; and the window's CSP carries `require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types default`, so your applet must not register a Trusted Types policy of its own, `default` or any other name. Libraries that create one need a fallback.

**Consent for destructive kinds.** When your applet asks the shell to sign a replaceable event (kind 0, 3 or 10000–19999), an addressable event (30000–39999), a deletion (5) or a request to vanish (62), through `relay.publish` or `outbox.publish`, kernl looks up the version it replaces (for up to 4 seconds on the network), shows the user a summary of what changes and waits. Expect the publish to take as long as a person takes to read. If they refuse, signing fails with `denied:consent` and nothing is published; you receive the normal error envelope. Every other kind is signed without a prompt, and nothing is remembered: the next destructive write asks again.

None of this changes the wire format. A refusal is a normal NAP error envelope; a guard event is visible to the user, not to your applet.

## Test against the guard

You can exercise the guard's layers without the full shell, because `@kernl/guard` is pure. The packages are not yet on npm, so this needs a clone of the kernl source ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)). The visibility gate below is the layer that holds a hidden window's `hello`; the ingress guard is the one that counts and quarantines.

```ts
import { createGuardConfig, createIngressGuard, createVisibilityGate, type GuardEvent } from '@kernl/guard';

const events: GuardEvent[] = [];
const config = createGuardConfig('strict');
const guard = createIngressGuard({ config, onEvent: (event) => events.push(event) });
const gate = createVisibilityGate({ config, onEvent: (event) => events.push(event) });

gate.setVisibility('w1', { visible: false, focused: false });
if (gate.shouldDefer('w1', 'relay:subscribe')) gate.defer('w1', { type: 'relay.subscribe', size: 512 });
// held; gate.drain('w1') returns it once the window is visible again

gate.setVisibility('w1', { visible: true, focused: true });
for (let i = 0; i < 9; i += 1) {
  guard.admit('w1', 'my-applet', { type: 'relay.publish', kind: 1 }, gate.getVisibility('w1'));
}
// the ninth call inside one second returns 'defer' and emits { disposition: 'defer', reason: 'flood:burst' }
```

Pass `now: () => clock` to both factories to drive time from the test instead of the wall clock. `createFocusFirewall({ config })` adds the per-class rates on top; its `observe()` returns kehto's `EvaluateResult`.

Scenarios worth writing for your own applet:

1. Mount hidden, then show: your UI settles whether replies arrived while hidden or after.
2. Lose focus mid-operation: your publish completes or fails cleanly; nothing is retried twice.
3. Hit a rate limit on purpose: your applet shows the user something useful instead of a stack trace.
4. Be declined: require nothing you cannot explain in the one line the launcher shows.
5. New build, old user: your applet's new hash has no grants. Make the first run after an update as good as the first run ever.

## Run it in kernl

[Write an applet](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/write-an-applet.md) walks through this end to end with a minimal applet. In short: follow [Run the shell](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/run-the-shell.md), publish your applet with the napplet tooling to a relay in the shell's `apps` tier (by default `wss://relay.napplet.soy`), click **Open an applet** and paste its address. The launcher shows which switches your `requires` and `optional` produced. The guard panel (*Guard · strict · N* in the desktop bar) lists every guard event your applet triggered as a sentence that names the applet, what happened and why ("Applet … went over a limit: too many publishes" for `rate:relay:publish`; kernl reports these, and the runtime's rates do the refusing); the window's grants panel shows how many guard events it has had this session. Together they are the fastest feedback you will get on posture.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md -->

# Architecture

kernl is three layers. kehto supplies the primitives, four kernl packages supply the opinions, and one app renders them. Nothing in a lower layer knows about a higher one.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  apps/web  (@kernl/web)                        Astro 7 + Svelte 5    │
│  landing site at /         shell at /app/      docs at /docs/        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  @kernl/core                                   composition root      │
│  createKernl · applesauce adapters · decodePointer → resolve →       │
│  plan → mount · guard pipeline · grants · describeChange · layouts   │
│       │                 │                   │                        │
│  @kernl/guard      @kernl/messaging     @kernl/bridges               │
│  ingress, gate,    provider contract,   locators, Bridge contract,   │
│  focus firewall,   registry, composite  registry, HTTP bridge        │
│  CSP, profiles     dm adapter           with SSRF policy             │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  kehto   @kehto/shell · runtime · acl · firewall · services · nip ·  │
│          wm                                                          │
│  applesauce   EventStore · RelayPool · AccountManager · signers ·    │
│               loaders                                                │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  @napplet/core   NAP wire types, NapDomain, envelope dispatch        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## The kehto layer

kehto is the runtime authority for how a NIP-5D shell composes. kernl uses these seams unchanged:

| kehto package | What kernl takes from it |
| --- | --- |
| `@kehto/shell` | `createShellBridge`, `buildShellCapabilities`, `resolveShellEnvironment`, `prepareNappletSrcdoc`, `denyNappletControllerAccess`, `renderNappletFramePolicyMeta`, `originRegistry`, the `ShellAdapter` hooks and the revocation model. |
| `@kehto/runtime` | The protocol engine behind the bridge: dispatch, the ACL gate (`bridge.runtime.aclState`, `ALL_CAPABILITIES`), the runtime firewall (`bridge.runtime.firewallState`), the `ServiceRegistry` and `ConsentRequest`. |
| `@kehto/acl` | The grant store the runtime enforces, keyed by `dTag:hash`. kernl reaches it only through `bridge.runtime.aclState`. |
| `@kehto/firewall` | The pure `evaluate()` engine `@kernl/guard` runs, and the `NappletRules` and `RateLimit` types `runtimeFirewallRules` translates into. |
| `@kehto/services` | `createRelayPoolService`, `createIdentityService`, `createThemeService`, `createNotifyService`, `createLinkService`, `createResourceService`, `createDmService`, `createOutboxService` and `createRelayPoolOutboxRouter`. |
| `@kehto/nip` | `resolveNapplet`, `openNappletArtifactCache` and `NAPPLET_KINDS` from `@kehto/nip/5d`. |
| `@kehto/wm` | `LayoutStrategy`, `WindowState`, `Rect` and `WindowPlacement`, which the layouts implement. |

kernl never re-implements a kehto primitive. When a seam is too narrow, kernl composes in front of it and takes the gap upstream; the four gaps found so far, filed upstream as kehto/web #397–#400, are in [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#upstream-gaps).

## One event layer

Every relay connection, event store, signer, account and loader goes through applesauce v7 ([D-002](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-002)). `createKernl` creates exactly one of each per shell, or uses the one the host passes in:

| Instance | Role | Adapted by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EventStore` | The in-memory, reactive store of every event the shell knows. Applets never receive a reference; `createIdentityProviders` (`applesauce/identity-providers.ts`) and `lookupReplaceable` read from it on their behalf. | kehto's identity service and the consent handler. |
| `RelayPool` | Every relay connection. | `createRelayPoolHooks` and `createRelayPoolLike` (`applesauce/relay-hooks.ts`) for `ShellAdapter.relayPool`; `createAppletRelayBackend`, `createDmRelayPool` and `createOutboxRelayPool` (`applesauce/relay-backend.ts`) for the relay, dm and outbox services. All of them route through `selectRelayTier`. |
| `AccountManager` | The signed-in accounts and their signers. | `createKernlAccounts` (`applesauce/accounts.ts`) refuses plaintext-key account types; `createAuthHooks` and `wrapAccountSigner` (`applesauce/auth-hooks.ts`) give kehto a signer that never reveals the account. |

`nostr-tools` is a peer dependency of `@kernl/core`, because kehto and applesauce require it. kernl source never imports it, and `scripts/check-dependency-rules.mjs` fails the build if it does.

## The kernl packages

| Package | Depends on | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`@kernl/guard`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/guard.md) | `@kehto/firewall` | Flood control, visibility gate, focus-aware firewall, CSP profile, mitigation descriptions. Pure: no DOM, no timers, time is injected. |
| [`@kernl/messaging`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/messaging.md) | `@napplet/core` (types) | The provider contract and the composite backend. Structurally identical to kehto's `DmAdapter` so a composite can be handed to `createDmService` without translation, while the package stays free of a kehto dependency. |
| [`@kernl/bridges`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/bridges.md) | nothing | Locator parsing, the `Bridge` contract, the registry with its `authorize` hook, the HTTP bridge. |
| [`@kernl/core`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md) | all of the above, kehto, applesauce | Composition: adapters, the applet lifecycle, the guard pipeline and runtime firewall rules, grants, consent summaries, layouts, the namespaced store. Browser-agnostic; the DOM is reached through `KernlHost` and `FrameLike`. |

The three leaf packages have zero framework dependencies and import nothing from each other. Only `core` composes them. The dependency rules are enforced by `pnpm check:deps`.

## Where each NAP domain is served from

An applet reaches the shell through the NAP domains in `window.napplet`. `createKernlServices` (`kernl-services.ts`) registers eight kehto services; `shell`, `inc`, `storage`, `keys` and `media` are routed by kehto's runtime itself. What one applet sees is `buildShellCapabilities(adapter).domains` narrowed by `createEnvironmentResolver(grants)`.

| NAP domain | Served by | kernl supplies | Guarded by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `shell`, `inc` | kehto runtime | the environment from `resolveShellEnvironment`, narrowed per identity | identity binding; baseline, no grant needed |
| `storage` | kehto runtime | the ACL state quota (`grants.setStateQuota`) | baseline; rate `storage:write` |
| `identity` | `createIdentityService` | the active signer through `createAuthHooks`; profile, follows, mutes and relays from `createIdentityProviders` | grant (`identity:read`), "your account" in the shell |
| `theme` | `createThemeService` | `KernlOptions.theme` when `isTheme` accepts it | baseline |
| `relay` | `createRelayPoolService` | `createAppletRelayBackend` over the one pool, routed by `selectRelayTier` | grant; rates `relay:subscribe`, `relay:publish`; subscribe envelope cap |
| `outbox` | `createOutboxService` | `createRelayPoolOutboxRouter` over `createOutboxRelayPool`, relay lists from `createIdentityProviders`, signing through the active signer (`denied:read-only` without one) | grant; rates `outbox:subscribe`, `outbox:publish`; consent for destructive kinds |
| `resource` | `createResourceService` | `createBridgeResourceResolver(bridges)` with the requesting applet named through `resourceInitFor` | grant; rate `resource:bytes`, resource envelope cap, hidden resource allowance, SSRF policy |
| `dm` | `createDmService` | `messaging.composite()` | grant; rate `dm:send`; provider availability |
| `notify` | `createNotifyService` | `host.notify` with tone `info` | grant |
| `link` | `createLinkService` | `host.openLink` after `LINK_PROTOCOLS` (`https:`, `mailto:`) allowed it | grant |
| `keys`, `media` | kehto runtime | nothing: hotkeys are not forwarded and no media hook is wired | grant |

So the shell offers thirteen domains: the baseline `shell`, `inc`, `theme` and `storage`, and `identity`, `relay`, `outbox`, `resource`, `dm`, `notify`, `link`, `keys` and `media` behind a grant. Domains kernl does not serve (`config`, `cvm`, `upload`, `intent`, `fs`, `llm`, `cache`) have a row in `DOMAIN_CAPABILITIES` so a grant can be expressed, but the shell does not offer them and `grants.allowDomain` refuses them with `invalid:domain`. [Identity and grants](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md) explains how the set is narrowed.

## The mount path

`createAppletLifecycle` (`kernl-lifecycle.ts`) turns an address into a running window in four steps, and the order is load-bearing:

1. **`decodePointer(input)`** (`applets/pointer.ts`) turns the address into `{ kind: 'address' | 'event', … }` and nothing more. Trust comes from verifying the event, never from the pointer.
2. **`resolve(pointer)`** fetches the manifest from the pointer's relay hints plus the `apps` tier (`fetchManifestEvent`), then verifies the signature and the artifact bytes by hash through `resolveApplet` over kehto's `resolveNapplet` (`applets/resolve.ts`). Cached bytes are re-hashed on every read. Gateways and caches are accelerators, never identity.
3. **`plan(summary)`** calls `grants.ensure(identity)`, then `planMount` (`applets/plan.ts`): it refuses markup that declares a frame (`denied:nested-frame`), then builds the environment from `resolveShellEnvironment`, the guard's CSP and the namespace prelude inserted by `prepareNappletSrcdoc`, the Trusted Types directives and frame lock spliced in after them ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)), `sandbox: 'allow-scripts'`, and `missingRequired`.
4. **`mount(plan, frame)`** installs the profile's rates in kehto's runtime firewall with `applyRuntimeFirewallRules`, then `mountApplet` (`applets/mount.ts`) hardens the frame, registers the window in `originRegistry`, sets the environment, calls `bridge.observeFrame`, and only then assigns `srcdoc`. The frame has `sandbox="allow-scripts"` and `denyNappletControllerAccess` applied; it never has `src` and never `allow-same-origin`.

Every revocation reason (`window-message`, `second-hello`, `invalid-hello`, `second-load`, `port-closed`, `host`) and a guard quarantine removes the iframe and drops the guard's state for that window. [Security posture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/security-posture.md) lists the rules this path must keep.

## The app

`apps/web` is Astro 7 with Svelte 5 islands. It owns the landing site at `/`, the shell at `/app/`, and the `KernlHost` that gives `@kernl/core` a page: `localStorage`, the consent dialog, notices, link confirmation and window visibility. It creates the iframes, wires `window.addEventListener('message', kernl.handleWindowMessage)` once, and renders the launcher, the grants panel per window, the guard panel and the provider picker. The published packages contain none of this; the app is the only framework-dependent workspace ([D-004](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-004)). `?preview=1` swaps in `preview-kernl.ts`, which implements the same `Kernl` contract without a network ([D-011](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-011)).

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md -->

# Bridges

Nostr is kernl's identity and resolution layer. It is not the only protocol kernl speaks. A bridge is a shell-owned service that resolves a protocol-specific locator to bytes, a job or a conversation, behind the same grant and quota as everything else: an applet needs the `resource` grant, and the guard's rates apply to its requests. There is no per-request bridge consent in this draft. Bridges are named by what they do for the user, never by the protocol they speak ([D-010](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-010)).

## Locators

A `Locator` is a parsed address: a lowercase `scheme` without the colon, the `raw` string, and scheme-specific `fields`, each a string or a list of strings. `parseLocator(uri)` produces it.

| Scheme | Fields | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `https`, `http`, `ws`, `wss` | `origin`, `host` (with port when present), `path` (pathname plus query, no fragment) | `HTTPS://Example.com:8443/a/b?c=1#frag` gives scheme `https`, origin `https://example.com:8443`, host `example.com:8443`, path `/a/b?c=1`. A web URL whose path ends in `.nzb` is parsed as an `nzb` locator instead. |
| `magnet` | `infoHash` (40 lowercase hex; a 32-character base32 hash is normalised to hex), `name` (from `dn`, absent when not given), `trackers` (list from every `tr`), `webSeeds` (list from every `ws`) | A magnet without a `urn:btih:` hash of either length fails with `invalid:magnet-missing-hash`. |
| `nzb` | `url` (the `http:` or `https:` document URL), `name` (the URL's `name` query parameter, else its last path segment, decoded) | Two spellings: `nzb://` followed by the URL-encoded document URL, or any web URL ending in `.nzb`. A wrapped URL with another scheme fails with `invalid:locator`. |
| `slsk` | `user`, `path` (both decoded) | `slsk://user/path/to/file`. Both parts are required; `slsk://ada`, `slsk://ada/` and `slsk:///path` fail with `invalid:locator`. |
| `mailto` | `address` (the decoded address part as written), `addresses` (list split on `,` and trimmed), `subject` and `body` (only when present) | `mailto:?subject=Hello` fails with `invalid:locator`. |
| anything else | none | `ftp://files.example/pub/x` is a locator with scheme `ftp` and no fields; the registry will report `unavailable:no-bridge` for it. |

Strings without a scheme (`just words`, `/relative/path`, `1abc:not-scheme`, the empty string) fail with `invalid:locator`. `isNzbUrl(url)` is the test the parser uses for the `.nzb` route. `formatLocator(locator)` returns a label without the scheme: the magnet `name` or else the hash, the NZB `name`, the last segment of the Soulseek path or else the user, the mail addresses joined with `, `, the web `host`, or the raw string after its scheme for unknown schemes. See `locators.feature`.

## The bridge contract

```ts
import type { BridgeAvailability, BridgeContext, BridgeExposure, BridgeResult, Locator } from '@kernl/bridges';

interface Bridge {
  readonly id: string;                 // 'http' | 'torrent' | 'nzb' | 'soulseek' | 'mail'
  readonly label: string;              // 'downloads' | 'sharing' | 'mail'
  readonly schemes: readonly string[];
  readonly exposure: BridgeExposure;
  availability(): BridgeAvailability;
  resolve(locator: Locator, context: BridgeContext): Promise<BridgeResult>;
}
```

`resolve` receives a `BridgeContext`: the `requester` (a verified applet identity `{ dTag, hash }`, or `'shell'` for the user's own request), an optional `AbortSignal` and optional headers. It returns one of three `BridgeResult` shapes:

| `kind` | Payload | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bytes` | a `Response` | HTTP |
| `job` | `{ id, label }` for a long-running transfer | torrent, NZB, Soulseek |
| `conversation` | `{ id, participants }` | mail |

## Exposure descriptions

The user sees a bridge before they use it, and what they see is its `BridgeExposure`: three booleans, rendered as plain sentences by `describeBridge`.

| Field | Row label | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `revealsAddress` | Shares your network address | Does the remote party learn the user's network address? |
| `encryptedInTransit` | Encrypted in transit | Is the transfer encrypted on the wire? |
| `publicActivity` | Activity visible to others | Can other participants see what the user is fetching? |

`describeBridge(bridge)` returns, in order: `Used for` (the label), `Status` (`ready`, or `not available` followed by a `Reason` row with the bare reason such as `no-backend`), then the three exposure rows as `yes`/`no`. A bridge whose availability is `{ available: true, handoff: true }` gets two more rows after `Status: ready`: `Handled by: an app on your device` and `Sent through kernl: no`. The exposure rows stay as they are for a hand-off bridge, because the app on the device speaks the same protocol and exposes the user the same way ([Hand-off backends](#hand-off-backends)). No row names a protocol. These are descriptions, not scores; like messaging providers, bridges are not ranked. See `describe.feature`.

## The registry and its authorize hook

The shell holds one `BridgeRegistry`, built with `createBridgeRegistry({ authorize?, onResolve? })`:

- `register(bridge)` adds a bridge. A second bridge with the same id throws `invalid:duplicate-bridge <id>`; a bridge claiming a scheme another bridge serves throws `invalid:scheme-taken <scheme>`. Schemes are compared lowercase with any trailing colon removed.
- `forScheme(scheme)` finds the bridge that serves a scheme, with the same normalisation (`NZB:` finds the `nzb` bridge).
- `resolve(uri, context)` parses, routes, checks availability, authorises and resolves, in that order, and stops at the first failure.

| Step | Failure reason | `BridgeResolveEvent.bridge` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| parse | `invalid:locator`, `invalid:magnet-missing-hash` | `none`, scheme `""` |
| route | `unavailable:no-bridge` | `none` |
| availability | `unavailable:<reason>` from the bridge | the bridge id |
| authorise | `denied:bridge` | the bridge id |
| resolve | whatever the bridge threw (`denied:…`, `unavailable:…`, `invalid:…`); a non-`Error` rejection is reported as its text | the bridge id |

Every outcome, successful or not, is reported to `onResolve` as `{ bridge, scheme, ok, reason? }`, when the registry was given one. The composed shell gives none, so bridge outcomes reach neither the guard panel nor any other surface the user sees. The authoriser is a `BridgeAuthorizer`: `(locator, bridge, context) => boolean | Promise<boolean>`. Without one, every request is allowed. The composed shell has none: `createKernl` builds its registry with `createDefaultBridges({ handoff: (uri) => host.openLink(uri) })` and no `authorize`, so a `resource` request from an applet that holds the `resource` grant is checked by the HTTP bridge's policy and nothing else. There is no per-host consent prompt and no per-host grant in this draft ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#what-does-not-work-yet)); wiring one is on the [Roadmap](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md#_6-guard). A host can pass its own registry with an `authorize` hook in `KernlOptions.bridges`. See `registry.feature`.

## The HTTP bridge

`createHttpBridge({ policy?, fetch?, resolveHost? })` is complete and serves the `resource` NAP domain. Its id is `http`, its label `downloads`, and its `HttpPolicy` is `DEFAULT_HTTP_POLICY` with any `policy` overrides merged in:

| Field | Default | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowedSchemes` | `['https:']` (`URL.protocol` form, colon included) | Plain HTTP would make `encryptedInTransit` a lie. |
| `maxRedirects` | `3` | Enough for a CDN hop; too few for a redirect loop to be useful. |
| `maxBytes` | `10485760` (10 MiB) | Larger payloads belong to a `job` bridge, not to an applet's memory. |
| `timeoutMs` | `20000` | A slow origin should fail visibly, not hold the window's resource budget. |
| `allowPrivateHosts` | `[]` | Private-address block on by default. |

The bridge's `schemes` and `exposure` follow the policy: with the default it serves `https` only and declares `revealsAddress: true`, `encryptedInTransit: true`, `publicActivity: false`. A shell that adds `'http:'` to `allowedSchemes` gets a bridge that serves `https` and `http` and declares `encryptedInTransit: false` (`http-bridge.feature`, scenario "the shell can admit the unencrypted scheme and the bridge says so").

Before every request, including every redirect hop, the bridge checks the URL. A scheme outside the policy fails with `denied:scheme <protocol>`. A host that `isBlockedHostname` or `isPrivateAddress` recognises fails with `denied:private-address <host>`, unless it is listed in `allowPrivateHosts`. When `resolveHost` is supplied, the host's addresses are checked too and a private one fails with `denied:private-address <host> -> <ip>`. No caller supplies it in this draft: `createDefaultBridges()` creates the HTTP bridge without `http.resolveHost`, so the composed shell judges a hostname by `isBlockedHostname` and `isPrivateAddress` on the literal alone. A public name that resolves to a private address is not caught, and there is no DNS-rebinding protection. Even with a resolver, the fetch API cannot pin a connection to the validated address, so the check would narrow the rebinding window without closing it.

| Check | Blocked |
| --- | --- |
| `isPrivateAddress`, IPv4 | `0.0.0.0/8`, `10.0.0.0/8`, `100.64.0.0/10`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `169.254.0.0/16`, `172.16.0.0/12`, `192.0.0.0/24` (IETF protocol assignments), `192.168.0.0/16`, `198.18.0.0/15` (benchmarking), `224.0.0.0/3` (multicast, reserved and broadcast) |
| `isPrivateAddress`, IPv6, judged by the embedded IPv4 address | IPv4-compatible `::/96` (which covers `::` and `::1`), IPv4-mapped `::ffff:0:0/96`, IPv4-translated `::ffff:0:0:0/96` and the well-known NAT64 prefix `64:ff9b::/96`: the low 32 bits are checked against the IPv4 list above, so `::ffff:127.0.0.1` is blocked and a NAT64 address for a public host is not |
| `isPrivateAddress`, IPv6, blocked outright | link-local `fe80::/10`, deprecated site-local `fec0::/10`, unique-local `fc00::/7`, multicast `ff00::/8`, discard-only `100::/64`, local-use NAT64 `64:ff9b:1::/48`, and the tunnelling prefixes 6to4 `2002::/16` and Teredo `2001::/32`, whose embedded IPv4 address the bridge cannot vouch for |
| `isBlockedHostname` | `localhost` and any name under `.localhost`, `.local` or `.internal`, case-insensitively, trailing dot ignored |

An IPv6 literal is parsed to its full 128 bits before it is judged: `::` is expanded, a dotted IPv4 tail is converted, brackets and a zone suffix (`%eth0`) are stripped, and case is ignored. Every spelling of an address is therefore judged the same way, including the hex form `new URL` normalises `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` to (`::ffff:7f00:1`). Strings that are neither a valid IPv4 nor a valid IPv6 literal (`1.2.3`, `256.1.1.1`, `1::2::3`, `example.com`) are not addresses and pass `isPrivateAddress`; a hostname is judged by `isBlockedHostname` and, only if a resolver was supplied, by what it resolves to. The shell supplies none, so in the composed shell the check is literal-only.

Every request is made with `redirect: 'manual'`, so the bridge decides about each hop itself. What that yields depends on where the bridge runs:

- **In Node and on servers**, a `301`, `302`, `303`, `307` or `308` response carries its `Location`. The bridge follows it by hand, up to `maxRedirects` hops, and each hop passes the same scheme and host checks. More than `maxRedirects` hops fails with `denied:too-many-redirects`; a redirect without a usable `Location` fails with `invalid:redirect`.
- **In a browser**, which is where the shell runs, `fetch` with `redirect: 'manual'` returns an opaque redirect (`type: 'opaqueredirect'`, status 0) whose target the bridge cannot read. It cannot re-check the next hop, so it refuses the request with `denied:redirect-unverifiable` instead of following blind. A URL that redirects does not load from the shell in this draft; ask for the final URL.

Browser requests are also subject to CORS: the shell's page fetches the URL, so an origin that does not allow cross-origin reads fails, and the browser does not say why. A request the browser blocks, for CORS or because the network failed, surfaces as `unavailable:network Failed to fetch`; any other status-0 answer as `unavailable:network <type> response`, for example `unavailable:network opaque response`. In practice the web bridge in the shell works for `https` origins that permit cross-origin reads and answer without a redirect. Requests race `AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs)` and the caller's signal: the time limit fails with `unavailable:timeout`, a caller cancel with `unavailable:aborted`, any other fetch failure with `unavailable:network <message>`. Caller headers are forwarded on every hop.

A response whose `content-length` exceeds `maxBytes` fails with `denied:too-large` before the body is read. Otherwise the `Response` is returned with its status and headers, and its body is streamed through a counter that errors the stream with `denied:too-large` the moment the limit is crossed. Before the request reaches the bridge, kehto's runtime firewall applies the `resource:fetch` rate kernl installed at mount and refuses a request over budget. kernl's guard sees the envelope just before kehto dispatches it but cannot hold it: `maxResourceEnvelopeBytes` and the focus firewall's `resource:bytes` bucket only report, while a hidden window's request past `hiddenResourceAllowance` quarantines the applet, and that request is not dispatched ([Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#where-enforcement-happens)).

## Backend-driven bridges

Four bridges are complete up to the backend interface they call. Each takes its backend as an optional argument.

| Bridge id | Label | Scheme | Reveals address | Encrypted in transit | Public activity | Backend interface | Call made |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `torrent` | `downloads` | `magnet` | yes | no | yes | `TorrentBackend` | `add(infoHash, trackers, context, name?) → { id, name }` |
| `nzb` | `downloads` | `nzb` | yes | yes | no | `NzbBackend` | `add(url, context) → { id, name }` |
| `soulseek` | `sharing` | `slsk` | yes | no | yes | `SoulseekBackend` | `download(user, path, context) → { id, name }` |
| `mail` | `mail` | `mailto` | no | yes | no | `MailBackend` | `open(address, subject \| undefined, context, body?) → { id }` |

The first three return `{ kind: 'job', id, label: name }`; the mail bridge returns `{ kind: 'conversation', id, participants: addresses }`. Fields are read from the locator before the backend is called; a locator missing one rejects with `invalid:locator-missing-<field>` (`backend-bridges.feature`, scenario "a locator missing a required field is rejected before the backend is called").

Every backend interface extends `BackendTraits`, whose one field is `handoff?: true`. A bridge reports:

| Backend | `availability()` | `resolve()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| none | `{ available: false, reason: 'no-backend' }` | rejects with `unavailable:no-backend` |
| one that moves data itself | `{ available: true }` | calls the backend |
| one with `handoff: true` | `{ available: true, handoff: true }` | calls the backend, which opens an app on the device |

Nothing pretends to work: a bridge without a backend says so in its status and reason.

### Hand-off backends

`createHandoffBackends(open)` returns `{ torrent, soulseek, mail, nzb }`, one backend for each bridge, all with `handoff: true`. Each rebuilds the locator's canonical address from the fields kernl parsed, so the address it opens carries only what kernl understood, and passes it to `open` once:

| Backend | Opens | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `torrent` | `magnet:?xt=urn:btih:<infoHash>`, then `&dn=<name>` when a name was given and one `&tr=<tracker>` per tracker, each value URL-encoded. Web seeds are dropped. | job labelled with the name, else the hash |
| `soulseek` | `slsk://<user>/<path>`, with the user and each path segment URL-encoded | job labelled with the last path segment, else the user |
| `mail` | `mailto:<address>`, then `?subject=…&body=…` for those present | conversation with the parsed addresses |
| `nzb` | the document's `https` URL itself, so the device's NZB client or browser takes it. A document served over plain `http` is refused with `invalid:nzb-not-https` and nothing is opened. | job labelled with the last path segment, else the host |

The four share one counter, so successive hand-offs get ids `handoff:1`, `handoff:2` and so on. The backend awaits `open` before it reports the result. `HandoffOpener` is `(uri: string) => void | Promise<void>`. See `handoff-backends.feature`.

`createDefaultBridges` takes an optional `handoff` opener. With one, it builds the torrent, NZB, Soulseek and mail bridges over `createHandoffBackends(handoff)`; without one, those four report `no-backend` as before. `createKernl` passes `host.openLink`, so all four are available in the live shell. The shell's `openLink` asks the user to confirm before leaving kernl ("Leave kernl and open this link?") and then opens the address in a new browsing context with `noopener,noreferrer`, which the browser hands to whatever app the device registers for the scheme. If the user declines, nothing is opened, but `openLink` does not report the refusal, so the bridge still returns its job or conversation.

What the user is exposed to:

- **kernl's network sees nothing.** For a hand-off, kernl makes no connection: no swarm, indexer, news server, peer or mail provider is contacted by the shell or by any applet. The address is the only thing that leaves kernl, and it leaves to the device, not to the network.
- **The device app's behaviour is outside kernl.** The torrent client, the Soulseek client, the mail program or the NZB downloader then does what it does, with its own settings and its own network. The exposure rows describe what that protocol normally exposes, which is why they stay the same as for an in-shell backend, but kernl cannot see, limit or revoke what the app does. If no app is registered for the scheme, the browser decides what happens.

### In-shell backends

A backend that moves the data inside the shell, such as a WebTorrent client, replaces the hand-off backend for its bridge: build the bridge with your backend in place of the hand-off one. The bridge then reports `{ available: true }`, the `Handled by` and `Sent through kernl` rows disappear, and the traffic is the shell's. Supplying one is a shell change plus a docs change; see [Add a bridge backend](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/add-a-bridge-backend.md). The order in which in-shell backends are planned is in the [Roadmap](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md#_2-bridge-backends).

## The resource resolver

kehto's resource service takes a `fetch(url, init)` function. `createBridgeResourceResolver(registry, { requesterFor? })` returns one over the registry. The requester is `init.requester` when the service names it, else `requesterFor(init)` when the shell supplied a way to derive it (for example from the window id), else `'shell'`. `init.signal` and `init.headers` reach the bridge. A `bytes` result is returned as its `Response`; a `job` or `conversation` result becomes `Response.json(result, { status: 202 })` so the caller can show progress; a failure rejects with the registry's prefixed reason, which the service maps to its error envelope. See `resource-resolver.feature`.

## Error reasons

| Reason | Thrown by |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid:locator` | `parseLocator` for anything that is not a locator or a malformed web, NZB, Soulseek or mail locator |
| `invalid:magnet-missing-hash` | `parseLocator` for a magnet without a `urn:btih:` hash |
| `invalid:locator-missing-<field>` | a backend-driven bridge whose locator lacks `infoHash`, `url`, `user`, `path` or `address` |
| `invalid:nzb-not-https` | the NZB hand-off backend, for a document not served over `https` |
| `invalid:duplicate-bridge <id>`, `invalid:scheme-taken <scheme>` | `BridgeRegistry.register` |
| `invalid:redirect` | HTTP bridge, redirect without a usable `Location` |
| `unavailable:no-bridge` | `BridgeRegistry.resolve`, no bridge serves the scheme |
| `unavailable:no-backend` | a backend-driven bridge without a backend (`availability().reason` is the bare `no-backend`) |
| `unavailable:timeout`, `unavailable:aborted`, `unavailable:network <message>` | HTTP bridge; in a browser a CORS refusal is `unavailable:network Failed to fetch`, another status-0 answer `unavailable:network <type> response` |
| `denied:bridge` | `BridgeRegistry.resolve`, the authoriser said no |
| `denied:scheme <protocol>`, `denied:private-address <host>`, `denied:private-address <host> -> <ip>`, `denied:too-many-redirects`, `denied:too-large` | HTTP bridge |
| `denied:redirect-unverifiable` | HTTP bridge in a browser, for an opaque redirect it cannot inspect |

## Why bridges are shell-owned

An applet could, in principle, be given a WebRTC or WebSocket path and speak these protocols itself. kernl does not allow that, because the CSP [never loosens](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#why-csp-never-loosens). Routing every protocol through a shell service means every protocol gets the same grant, the same quota, the same exposure description and the same revocation, and a consent prompt per request, which this draft does not have, could be added in one place. The applet asks for a locator; the user's `resource` grant decides whether it may; the shell does the talking.

## Related

- [`@kernl/bridges`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/bridges.md)
- [Security posture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/security-posture.md)
