<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md -->

# Guard

The guard is everything that stands between an applet and the user. Some of it is kehto's and kernl turns it on; some of it is kernl's and runs in front of kehto's bridge. The user sees it as one list of mitigations with reasons. This page is that list, with the numbers.

The rule from `SOUL.md`: if kehto ships a mitigation, kernl enables it by default and documents how to loosen it. The hosted shell boots `strict`, and there only the user loosens it ([D-003](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-003)). An embedding host may choose the starting profile (`KernlOptions.guard.profile`), which changes limits only; the sandbox, the CSP, the frame lock and consent are fixed. In this draft the profile is shell-wide and resets to `strict` on every boot; per-applet profiles are planned ([Roadmap](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md#_6-guard)).

**What refuses, what reports, what stops.** For an applet's port traffic, which is everything after the handshake, kehto's runtime firewall refuses an envelope before dispatch when it goes over the per-class rates kernl installs at mount, or over kehto's own startup burst. Size caps are refused before dispatch too: kernl measures the envelope and has the runtime firewall refuse that one dispatch. Otherwise kernl's ingress guard and focus firewall see each envelope synchronously, just before kehto dispatches it, but cannot hold or drop it: focus tightening, bursts above kernl's per-second rate and a hidden window's activity are reported as guard events, not refused. The exception is quarantine. When an envelope crosses the flood threshold, or a hidden window's download crosses its allowance, kernl revokes the binding inside the observation, so that envelope is not dispatched and the applet is closed ([Where enforcement happens](#where-enforcement-happens)). The visibility gate holds only the window-level `hello`. Signing consent is a third path, in the signer itself.

## The eleven mitigations

`describeMitigations(config)` in `@kernl/guard` returns this list as `MitigationDescription[]`, in this order, with the `limit` text computed from the profile in `config`. The shell renders it verbatim; the titles below are the ones the user sees, and they carry no protocol vocabulary. The third column is for developers and does.

| # | `id` | Title shown to the user | What it protects against | `provider` | `limit` in `strict` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `zero-network-sandbox` | Applets cannot reach the network on their own | Exfiltration, tracking pixels, loading code the user did not verify. The frame loads through `srcdoc` with `sandbox="allow-scripts"` and the CSP below, and kehto's prelude removes WebRTC before applet code runs. kernl refuses applet markup that declares a frame, and its frame lock stops applet code from creating one, so no child realm with a working peer connection can exist ([No network path](#no-network-path), [D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)). Every byte from the network arrives through a shell service. | `both` | none |
| 2 | `bound-identity` | An applet is only trusted while its connection and code match | A reloaded or substituted document inheriting grants, or one frame speaking for another. Identity is `(dTag, artifactHash)` plus the one `MessagePort` transferred in `napplet.hello`. Any other window-level message, a second `hello`, a `hello` without exactly one port, a second load or a closed port revokes the binding. | `kehto` | none |
| 3 | `verified-artifacts` | Applet code is verified before it runs, and again before reuse | A gateway or cache serving different code than the signed manifest names. Bytes are fetched by hash through `@kehto/nip/5d`, cached only after verification and re-verified on every read. | `kehto` | none |
| 4 | `replay-detection` | Old or repeated posts are not sent | The same signed post sent twice, or one dated to slip past a time window. kehto's replay detector runs on `relay.publish` after the shell signs: it refuses an event dated more than the replay window (30 s by default) in the past, more than 10 s in the future, or whose id it already saw inside the window. `outbox.publish` is not checked. A message from a window other than the applet's own is a port-binding matter, covered by `bound-identity`. | `kehto` | none |
| 5 | `rate-limits` | Applets have a budget for how often they can act | Publishing, subscribing or spending quota at a rate no human interaction explains. Refused before dispatch: kehto's runtime firewall refuses an over-budget envelope until the allowance refills, using the per-class rates kernl installs at mount, where deletions count against `relay:write`. The same firewall applies kehto's startup burst guard: more than 20 operations in a window's first 3 s are refused. kernl's focus firewall counts the classes again as each envelope arrives, including a separate `relay:publish:delete` bucket, and reports overruns as `rate:<class>` events. | `both` | `publish 20 per 60s, delete 5 per 60s, messages 20 per 60s` |
| 6 | `focus-tightening` | Applets you are not using are measured against a smaller budget | Background windows spending a foreground budget. Reported, not refused: kernl's focus firewall counts an unfocused window at `unfocusedMultiplier` of capacity as each envelope arrives and emits a guard event when it goes over, but the envelope is still dispatched. Focus is observed by the shell, never self-reported. The runtime firewall applies no unfocused multiplier at all: kehto's `ShellAdapter` does not forward `getFocusContext`, so the runtime treats every window as focused ([upstream gaps 1 and 4](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#upstream-gaps)). The rate-limits budget above still applies in full. | `kernl` | `25% of the focused budget` |
| 7 | `hidden-deferral` | Hidden applets that keep downloading are stopped | Hidden or minimised applets consuming network budget the user cannot see. Each `resource.*` request from a hidden window counts against `hiddenResourceAllowance` as it arrives; the one past it quarantines the window (`flood:hidden-resource`): the binding is revoked inside the observation, so that request is not dispatched, and the frame is removed. Other port traffic from a hidden window is recorded, not held. The visibility gate holds only a hidden window's window-level `hello`. | `kernl` | `8 downloads while hidden` |
| 8 | `ingress-flood` | Applets that flood the shell are put in quarantine | A busy loop starving the shell's main thread. Per-window token bucket, counted as each port envelope arrives: bursts above `ingressBurst` are reported (`flood:burst`, `flood:queue-full`) and still dispatched. The message that reaches `quarantineThreshold` in 10 s quarantines the window: the binding is revoked inside the observation, so that message is not dispatched, and the frame is removed. Only the window-level `hello` is actually queued or rejected. | `kernl` | `8 messages per second, 300 per 10s` |
| 9 | `size-caps` | Oversized requests are refused | Memory pressure from oversized filters or payloads. The ingress guard measures `resource.*` and `relay.subscribe`/`outbox.subscribe` envelopes as they arrive and rejects an oversized one with `size:<class>`. kehto's runtime cannot measure these itself (it sizes only an envelope's `event`), so kernl calls `refuseCurrentDispatch`, which sets the applet's runtime policy to `deny` for that one synchronous dispatch and restores it in a microtask. The applet receives a `firewall:` error, nothing is fetched, and the user sees the guard event. An oversized `hello` is dropped. | `both` | `downloads 64 KiB, queries 256 KiB` |
| 10 | `device-denial` | Applets cannot use your camera, microphone or other devices | An applet reaching hardware. `denyNappletControllerAccess` gives the frame the Permissions Policy `gamepad 'none'; hid 'none'; usb 'none'`; the frame's `allow` attribute delegates nothing else, so camera, microphone and other powerful features stay off. There is no grant for any of them. | `kehto` | none |
| 11 | `destructive-consent` | Deleting or overwriting asks you first | An applet acquiring authority the user did not knowingly give. `createSigningConsent` asks `host.presentConsent` before a destructive kind (every replaceable kind 0, 3, 10000–19999; every addressable kind 30000–39999; 5; 62) is signed for an applet, after looking up the current version in the store and then on the outbox and discovery relays for up to `CURRENT_VERSION_TIMEOUT_MS` (4000 ms); if none is found the summary says "Current version: could not be loaded; this replaces it entirely". It runs on both routes: the window signer from `ShellAdapter.auth.getSigner(windowId)` for `relay.publish`, and kernl's outbox gate for `outbox.publish`. A denial is `denied:consent` and nothing is signed; answers are not remembered, and the shell's own signing is not gated. kehto's runtime has no such step. | `kernl` | none |

`enabled` is `true` for every row in every profile; the field exists for the UI contract. Two things are not separate rows: the opaque-origin frame, the CSP and the frame lock are one row (`zero-network-sandbox`), and kehto's startup burst guard is part of `rate-limits`, because the same runtime firewall applies both ([What `burstGuard` is for](#layers)). See `mitigations.feature`, scenario "every mitigation is described once, in display order".

## Operation classes

kehto's firewall treats the operation class as an opaque key. `classifyEnvelope` gives each inbound envelope one of eleven classes from its `type` and, for publishes, its `kind`:

| Envelope type | Class |
| --- | --- |
| `relay.publish`, `relay.publishEncrypted` with `kind: 5` | `relay:publish:delete` |
| `relay.publish`, `relay.publishEncrypted` (any other kind) | `relay:publish` |
| `relay.subscribe` | `relay:subscribe` |
| `outbox.subscribe`, `outbox.query`, `outbox.getEvent` | `outbox:subscribe` |
| `outbox.publish` (any kind, including 5) | `outbox:publish` |
| `resource.*` | `resource:bytes` |
| `storage.set`, `storage.remove` | `storage:write` |
| `dm.send` | `dm:send` |
| `intent.invoke`, `intent.open` | `intent:invoke` |
| `relay.close`, `outbox.close`, `storage.get`, `storage.keys`, `shell.*`, `inc.*`, `theme.*`, `identity.*`, other `dm.*` | `control` |
| anything else (`clipboard.write`, …) | `generic` |

`relay:publish:delete` gives kind 5 deletions their own, tighter bucket in kernl's focus firewall, so a burst of deletes is reported as `rate:relay:publish:delete`. In the layer that refuses there is no separate delete bucket: kehto's runtime firewall keys by capability, and deletions share the `relay:write` budget with other publishes ([translation table](#where-enforcement-happens)). What stops an unwanted deletion is signing consent, not the rate. See `classification.feature`.

## Profiles

A profile is a `GuardLimits` record plus the derived kehto `FirewallConfig`; `createGuardConfig(profile)` builds both. Profiles change limits only. `GUARD_PROFILES` lists them tightest first.

| Limit | `strict` (default) | `balanced` | `relaxed` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ingressBurst` (messages per second before queueing) | 8 | 12 | 24 |
| `ingressQueue` (queued messages before rejection) | 64 | 128 | 192 |
| `quarantineThreshold` (messages per rolling 10 s before quarantine) | 300 | 420 | 800 |
| `hiddenResourceAllowance` (resource requests while hidden before quarantine) | 8 | 16 | 32 |
| `deferQueue` (held envelopes while hidden before rejection) | 200 | 400 | 600 |
| `maxResourceEnvelopeBytes` | 64 KiB (65 536) | 128 KiB (131 072) | 192 KiB (196 608) |
| `maxSubscribeEnvelopeBytes` | 256 KiB (262 144) | 512 KiB (524 288) | 768 KiB (786 432) |
| `unfocusedMultiplier` (rate capacity while unfocused) | 0.25 | 0.5 | 0.75 |

The per-class `rates` are a token-bucket capacity per window. `balanced` is exactly 2× `strict` and `relaxed` exactly 3×; the windows do not change.

| Class | Window | `strict` | `balanced` | `relaxed` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `relay:subscribe` | 60 s | 30 | 60 | 90 |
| `relay:publish` | 60 s | 20 | 40 | 60 |
| `relay:publish:delete` | 60 s | 5 | 10 | 15 |
| `outbox:subscribe` | 60 s | 30 | 60 | 90 |
| `outbox:publish` | 60 s | 20 | 40 | 60 |
| `resource:bytes` | 10 s | 120 | 240 | 360 |
| `storage:write` | 10 s | 60 | 120 | 180 |
| `dm:send` | 60 s | 20 | 40 | 60 |
| `intent:invoke` | 60 s | 10 | 20 | 30 |
| `control` | 10 s | 120 | 240 | 360 |
| `generic` | 10 s | 120 | 240 | 360 |

Every rate kernl registers in kehto has exceed action `block`; kehto's own default would be `flag`. The shell boots in `strict`. [Change the guard profile](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/change-guard-profile.md) shows how a user changes the shell-wide profile; per-applet profiles are planned. See `profiles.feature`.

## Layers

Three stateful objects, each built from the same `GuardConfig`, each keyed by `windowId`, each with a `forget(windowId)` to call on revocation. This section describes each layer's own API, which is what a caller that sits in front of dispatch gets. In the composed shell that is true only for the window-level `hello`; for port traffic the dispositions below become events and, for `quarantine`, a revocation that also stops the envelope that triggered it ([Where enforcement happens](#where-enforcement-happens)).

| Layer | Enforces | Factory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ingress guard | `ingressBurst`, `ingressQueue`, `quarantineThreshold`, `hiddenResourceAllowance`, both envelope size caps | `createIngressGuard({ config, now?, onEvent?, drainBatch? })` |
| Visibility gate | `deferQueue`; which classes wait while hidden | `createVisibilityGate({ config, now?, onEvent?, nappletFor? })` |
| Focus firewall | kehto `evaluate()`: per-applet class rates, the `generic` default rate, the content matchers, `unfocusedMultiplier`, per-applet policies | `createFocusFirewall({ config, now?, onEvent? })` |

**Ingress guard.** Each window has a token bucket of `ingressBurst` per second. While tokens remain, `admit` returns `pass`. When they are spent, or while anything is already queued, the envelope is queued and `admit` returns `defer` with reason `flood:burst`; nothing overtakes the queue. Past `ingressQueue` the envelope is rejected with `flood:queue-full`. `drain(windowId)` releases at most `drainBatch` (default 4) queued envelopes, never more than the refilled tokens allow, ordered `control` first, then `resource:bytes`, then everything else, oldest first within a rank. Arrivals are counted over a rolling `QUARANTINE_WINDOW_MS` (10 s); the arrival that reaches `quarantineThreshold` quarantines the window with `flood:quarantine`, drops its queue, and every later envelope returns `quarantine` with the same reason until `release(windowId)` (fresh budget, quarantine lifted) or `forget(windowId)`. While a window is hidden, each `resource:bytes` envelope counts against `hiddenResourceAllowance`; the one past it quarantines with `flood:hidden-resource`. Any admission while visible resets that count. An envelope whose class has a size cap and whose `size` exceeds it is rejected with `size:<class>`; an envelope without a `size` is not size-checked. A clock that runs backwards grants no tokens. See `ingress.feature`.

**Visibility gate.** The shell reports visibility with `setVisibility`; a window it has not reported on counts as visible and unfocused. `shouldDefer(windowId, opClass)` is true when the window is hidden and the class is not `control`, so a hidden window can still be closed, themed or asked for its identity. `defer` queues up to `deferQueue` envelopes and then returns `false` while emitting a `reject` event with reason `defer:queue-full`; the event names the applet through `nappletFor`, or `unknown` without one. `drain` returns every held envelope oldest first and empties the queue. Deferral is a privacy and resource measure, not a rate limit: a minimised applet should not fetch or publish while the user cannot see it. See `visibility.feature`.

**Focus firewall.** `observe` builds a kehto `Observation` from the envelope and the shell's `WindowVisibility` (`focused`, and `msSinceFocusGain` when known) and runs `evaluate()`. On the first observation of an applet it calls `applyNappletRules` so the applet's class rates exist in kehto's per-applet map; kehto keys those budgets by applet (`dTag`), so two windows of the same applet share a budget (`focus-firewall.feature`, scenario "budgets are per applet, not per window"). Decisions map to events: `reject` emits `reject`; `pass` with action `flag` emits `flag`; `prompt` emits `reject` with reason `prompt:<ruleId>`. kernl treats a prompt as a denial here because the layer has no UI; signing consent for destructive writes is a separate path, in the signer wrapper, not in the firewall. kehto's `rate:*` rule ids name the tier (`rate:opclass`, `rate:global`, `rate:default`); the event reason is rewritten to `rate:<class>` so the user sees what ran out. Other rule ids pass through unchanged, for example `matcher:size:resource:bytes` and `policy:deny`. In the composed shell a `matcher:size:*` event cannot occur: the ingress guard applies the same caps first, and the pipeline runs the focus firewall only for envelopes the ingress guard passed. `forget(windowId)` drops the buckets of every applet seen in that window, which also resets the budget of another window running the same applet; revocation is user-driven, so that is accepted.

**What `burstGuard` is for.** `createGuardConfig` sets `firewall.burstGuard` to `{ windowMs: 1000, maxOps: ingressBurst, action: 'block' }`. kehto's init-burst guard only fires for callers that supply `initElapsedMs` in the observation, and the focus firewall never does, so this field never fires inside `@kernl/guard`. The guard that does fire is the runtime's: kehto's runtime supplies `initElapsedMs` (time since the window's session registered) and evaluates its own configuration, kehto's default of 20 operations in the first 3 s with action `block`, because kernl installs rates in the runtime and nothing else. An applet that sends more than 20 envelopes in its first 3 s has the excess refused with a `firewall:` error.

## Where enforcement happens

kehto's bridge owns the `MessagePort` an applet speaks over and shows the host that traffic only through `ShellAdapter.onNappletMessage`. kehto's `dispatchEnvelope` calls that hook synchronously for each envelope, before it resolves the window's session and hands the envelope to the runtime, and ignores the hook's answer. kernl therefore observes every envelope before dispatch but cannot hold or drop it ([D-001](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-001)). Enforcement is layered ([D-012](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-012)):

| Traffic | Where | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The window-level `napplet.hello` | kernl, before kehto sees it | `Kernl.handleWindowMessage` resolves the sending window from `originRegistry`, never from the message, and runs ingress guard → visibility gate → focus firewall before `bridge.handleMessage`. This is the one message the pipeline can hold or drop; any other window-level message from a bound applet is kehto's `window-message` revocation. |
| Port traffic, observed | kernl, inside `onNappletMessage`, before dispatch | `onNappletMessage` feeds `GuardPipeline.observe`: the ingress guard and the focus firewall advance their counters and emit events, and the envelope continues to the runtime. A `quarantine` disposition calls `onQuarantine`, which marks the handle revoked with reason `quarantine` and calls `bridge.revokeNapplet(windowId, 'host')` while kehto is still inside the hook. kehto then finds no session for the window and does not dispatch the envelope, and the frame is removed. Quarantine is the only outcome here that stops an envelope. |
| Port traffic, refused by rate | kehto's runtime firewall, configured by kernl | `kernl.mount` calls `applyRuntimeFirewallRules(bridge.runtime.firewallState, config, dTag)`, which installs the profile's per-class rates and global rate for that applet. It sets no policy: kehto's `allow` policy would make `evaluate()` skip every rate, matcher and burst check. The runtime refuses over-budget envelopes, and envelopes past its startup burst, itself, before it handles them, and answers the applet with an error that starts `firewall:`. Rates are installed at mount: a window keeps the rates it was mounted with until it is opened again. |
| Port traffic, refused by size | kernl's ingress guard, enforced by kehto's runtime firewall | When the ingress guard emits `size:<class>` inside `onNappletMessage`, `createKernl` calls `refuseCurrentDispatch(bridge.runtime.firewallState, dTag)`: the applet's runtime policy is `deny` for the rest of that synchronous dispatch, so kehto refuses the envelope, and the previous policy returns in a microtask, before the next port message can arrive. |

The runtime keys its rates by the sender capability a message needs, while the guard classifies by what a message does. `RUNTIME_OP_CLASSES` translates:

| Guard class | Runtime key |
| --- | --- |
| `relay:subscribe` | `relay:read` |
| `relay:publish` | `relay:write` |
| `relay:publish:delete` | none; deletions share `relay:write` in the runtime and keep their own bucket only in kernl's focus firewall, which reports |
| `outbox:subscribe` | `outbox:read` |
| `outbox:publish` | `outbox:write` |
| `resource:bytes` | `resource:fetch` |
| `storage:write` | `state:write` |
| `dm:send` | `dm:write` |
| `intent:invoke` | `intent:write` |
| `control` | none; control envelopes need no capability |
| `generic` | the per-applet global rate (`setGlobalRate`) |

Two limits of this arrangement are stated plainly. The runtime firewall never applies an unfocused multiplier: kehto's `ShellAdapter` does not forward `getFocusContext`, so the runtime builds every observation as focused, and `FirewallStateContainer` has no setter for `unfocusedMultiplier` either. The profile's value (`0.25` in `strict`) is applied only by kernl's focus firewall, which reports. And hidden-window deferral is advisory for port traffic in this draft: the visibility gate holds only window-level messages, and `observe` cannot hold a port envelope, so for a hidden window the gate's effect is the tightened, reported budget, the hidden-resource allowance that quarantines, and the event trail, not a held queue. Both are recorded as upstream gaps in [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#upstream-gaps).

## Dispositions and reasons

`IngressGuard.admit()` returns one of four dispositions:

| Disposition | Meaning | For the window-level `hello` | For port traffic (observed, not held) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pass` | Within budget. | Forwarded to the bridge after the visibility gate and the focus firewall. | Nothing; the envelope is dispatched. |
| `defer` | The per-second burst is spent; the envelope is queued. | Held; `drainAll` forwards it as tokens refill. | A `flood:burst` event. The envelope is still dispatched. |
| `reject` | The queue is full or the envelope is over its size cap. | Dropped. | `flood:queue-full`: an event, and the envelope is still dispatched. `size:<class>`: an event, and the runtime firewall refuses the envelope (`refuseCurrentDispatch`). |
| `quarantine` | The window hit the quarantine threshold or the hidden resource allowance, or is still quarantined. | Dropped, and the window is revoked. | `onQuarantine` revokes the binding inside the hook, so this envelope is not dispatched, and the frame is removed. |

Every disposition other than `pass`, and every `pass` the firewall flagged, emits a `GuardEvent` with a stable prefixed reason. The user sees these events; secrets never appear in them.

| Reason | Emitted by | With disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flood:burst` | ingress guard | `defer` |
| `flood:queue-full` | ingress guard | `reject` |
| `flood:quarantine` | ingress guard | `quarantine` |
| `flood:hidden-resource` | ingress guard | `quarantine` |
| `size:<class>` (`size:resource:bytes`, `size:relay:subscribe`, `size:outbox:subscribe`) | ingress guard | `reject` |
| `defer:queue-full` | visibility gate | `reject` |
| `rate:<class>` | focus firewall | `reject`, or `flag` when the rate's action is `flag` |
| `matcher:<id>`, kehto's rule id passed through; the guard's own `matcher:size:*` matchers cannot fire in the composed shell, because the ingress guard rejects the same envelopes first | focus firewall | `reject` |
| `policy:deny` | focus firewall | `reject` |
| `prompt:<ruleId>` (`prompt:policy:ask`) | focus firewall | `reject` |

## Why CSP never loosens

The three profiles scale rates and queues. None of them touches the Content Security Policy. A profile is a statement about how much an applet may do through the shell; the CSP is a statement about whether an applet may bypass the shell at all. Loosening a rate limit lets a trusted applet work faster. Loosening the CSP would let it talk to the network directly, which removes the shell's ability to see, rate-limit and revoke that traffic and so removes every other mitigation on this page at once.

`createAppletCsp(profile)` therefore accepts the profile, so that callers configure one place, and ignores it. It returns `connectOrigins: []` and kehto's zero-network baseline of 14 directives, which `renderCsp` serialises as:

```
default-src 'none'; script-src 'unsafe-inline' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data: blob:; font-src data:; connect-src 'none'; worker-src 'none'; child-src 'none'; frame-src 'none'; media-src 'none'; object-src 'none'; manifest-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'
```

An applet that needs a network resource asks the `resource` domain, and the request goes through a [bridge](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md). See `csp.feature`, scenario "the relaxed profile does not loosen the CSP".

## No network path

`zero-network-sandbox` has three parts: the CSP, kehto's prelude, and kernl's frame lock.

**kehto's prelude.** `prepareNappletSrcdoc` puts it in the frame right after the CSP `<meta>`, so it runs before any applet code. Before it opens the port to the shell, the prelude takes every global whose name starts with `RTC`, plus `webkitRTCPeerConnection`, `mozRTCPeerConnection`, `webkitRTCSessionDescription`, `mozRTCSessionDescription`, `webkitRTCIceCandidate` and `mozRTCIceCandidate`, and redefines each as `undefined`, read-only, non-configurable and non-enumerable. The names still exist, but no value can be put back: `delete` and assignment leave them `undefined`. A peer connection would otherwise be a way out the CSP does not cover.

**kernl's frame lock** ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)). The prelude cleans only the applet's own realm. A child frame made from `srcdoc` or `about:blank` is a fresh realm with a working `RTCPeerConnection`, and no CSP directive reaches it, because creating it involves no fetch. `@kehto/shell` 0.29.0 has no switch for this; kehto's unreleased `experimental.nestedContextLock` closes it, and `@kernl/guard` carries an attributed port of that lock until a release ships it. `planMount` applies all of it to every applet:

- `assertAppletHasNoFrame` scans the verified bytes and refuses markup that contains an `iframe`, `frame`, `frameset`, `object`, `embed`, `portal` or `fencedframe` element with `denied:nested-frame`. It parses with the host's `DOMParser` and falls back to a lexical match, which may over-reject.
- `renderFrameLockScript()` is inserted immediately after kehto's prelude, before any applet script. It installs a Trusted Types `default` policy that refuses frame markup, namespace-prefixed tags included, at every HTML string sink (`innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, `createContextualFragment`, `DOMParser`), and pins `Document.prototype.createElement`, `createElementNS` and `DOMImplementation.prototype.createDocument` non-configurable so they throw `TypeError: denied:nested-frame` for a frame tag name.
- The same script runs `appletInsertionLock`, because creation routes are open-ended (custom element constructors, XSLT, namespace-prefixed XML parsing all mint frames without a factory) but a frame gets a realm only when it is connected. It pins every DOM insertion method (`appendChild`, `insertBefore`, `replaceChild`, `append`, `prepend`, `replaceChildren`, `before`, `after`, `replaceWith`, `insertAdjacentElement`, `moveBefore`, `Range.insertNode`, `Range.surroundContents`) to refuse a node that is, or contains, a frame element, reading node identity through native getters captured before applet code runs. It also refuses custom elements that extend frame elements and removes `XSLTProcessor`. Every insertion therefore walks the inserted subtree once.
- The CSP `<meta>` kehto rendered gains `TRUSTED_TYPES_DIRECTIVES`, `require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types default`, so every string sink goes through that policy and no other policy name can be registered. `createAppletCsp` carries the directives as `AppletCsp.trustedTypes`. kehto 0.29.0 refuses directives outside its baseline, so `planMount` appends them to the rendered meta, and refuses with `unavailable:frame-lock` when kehto's output is not where it expects it.

**The CSP** refuses everything else: `fetch` and WebSocket by `connect-src 'none'`, images by `img-src data: blob:`, frames that would load a URL by `frame-src 'none'` and `child-src 'none'`, and beacons by `connect-src`. `navigator.sendBeacon` still returns `true`, because it only reports that the beacon was queued; the request is refused when the browser sends it, and fails with `csp`.

`tests/e2e/applet-network-sealed.spec.ts` proves this in Chromium. It builds an applet frame with kernl's own `planMount` (`sandbox="allow-scripts"`, a host page carrying `KERNL_FRAME_POLICY_META`) and checks that the frame lock follows kehto's prelude and precedes the applet's script. The applet code then tries each way out, and the spec asserts:

- each of 15 frame-creation routes, plus `document.write` whole and split across calls, throws `TypeError: denied:nested-frame`; the four creation routes the factories cannot see (a customized built-in constructed with `new`, XSLT, and a namespace-prefixed XHTML element brought in with `importNode` or `adoptNode`) fail at creation or at insertion; and thirteen insertion routes (every pinned method, a shadow root, a fragment) refuse an unconnected frame;
- no child realm exists, no `RTC*` constructor is usable in the applet's realm, and no realm produces a `srflx` or `relay` ICE candidate. As a control, when the host page can reach a public STUN server, the spec asserts that it does and that the applet produces no such candidate; when it cannot, the control is skipped;
- `fetch` fails, the WebSocket never opens, every `RTC*` global is pinned to `undefined` and cannot be restored, the image does not load, the browser reports a CSP violation for each attempt including the beacon, and no request reaches the network layer: every outbound request fails with `csp`.

[D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014) records the negative control: the same probe run against a srcdoc built by kehto 0.29.0 alone lets 11 routes escape, each producing a child realm that reports `host` and `srflx` candidates.

## What the guard is not

It is not an access control list. Whether an applet may use a domain is a grant, described in [Identity and grants](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md). The guard assumes the grant exists and asks a different question: is this applet abusing what it was granted, right now?

## Related

- [`@kernl/guard`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/guard.md)
- [Change the guard profile](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/change-guard-profile.md)
- [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md)

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md -->

# Identity and grants

An applet is not a name. It is a specific set of verified bytes, running in one frame, speaking over one port. Grants attach to that, and die with it.

## Identity

kehto binds an applet's identity to two things, and kernl keeps both:

1. **The verified artifact hash.** `kernl.resolve` fetches the manifest event, verifies its signature, fetches the artifact bytes by SHA-256 and verifies them through kehto's `resolveNapplet` (`applets/resolve.ts`). The identity is `AppletIdentity`, `{ dTag, hash }`: `dTag` names the applet across versions, `hash` is kehto's `aggregateHash` and names this build. Cached bytes are re-hashed on every read. A gateway that serves different bytes produces a different hash, which is a different identity with no grants.
2. **The live message port.** The frame sends exactly one `napplet.hello` with exactly one transferred `MessagePort`. The bridge binds the identity to that port. Everything after the handshake travels over the port, never over `window.postMessage`.

The binding is revoked, the port closed and the iframe removed when the shell observes any of:

| Reason | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| `window-message` | A window-level message other than the one `napplet.hello`. |
| `second-hello` | A second `napplet.hello` from the same frame. |
| `invalid-hello` | A `hello` without exactly one transferred port. |
| `second-load` | The frame loaded a second document, by navigation or reload. |
| `port-closed` | The port closed or a message failed to deserialise. |
| `host` | The shell revoked the binding itself: the user closed the window (`handle.close()`), or the guard quarantined it, in which case `host.onRevoked` is told `quarantine`. |

A revoked window's identity can never be re-bound to the same iframe. Opening the applet again means a new frame, a new handshake and a fresh guard state. Grants, however, outlive the frame: they are keyed by identity, not by window.

## Grants

A grant is something the user gave and can take back. kehto's ACL holds, per `dTag:hash`, a capability set, a blocked flag and a state quota. kernl's `createGrants` (`grants/grants.ts`) keeps its own record per identity, `{ dTag, hash, domains, blocked }`, at `kernl:grants:v1`, and mirrors it into the ACL on every change. Two consequences:

- **A new build is a new grant.** When the applet's author publishes a new artifact, the hash changes and the grants for the old hash do not apply. The user approved specific code, not a name.
- **Grants are per applet, never global.** There is no "allow all applets to publish" switch. The user decides per `(dTag, hash)`, domain by domain.

A grant is expressed in domains, not capabilities. `DOMAIN_CAPABILITIES` (`grants/domain-capabilities.ts`) says which kehto capabilities a domain needs (`relay` is `relay:read` and `relay:write`; `shell` and `inc` need none), so the user is asked about `relay`, and the ACL receives both capabilities. The table is on the [core package page](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md#grants).

## Restrictive posture

kehto's `createRuntime` hardcodes the ACL default policy to `'permissive'`: a capability with no entry in the ACL store is allowed. kernl wants the opposite, and until the upstream gap in [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#upstream-gaps) is closed it produces the restrictive posture around the runtime in three places:

1. **Explicit ACL writes.** `KernlGrants.ensure(identity)` runs inside `kernl.plan`, before any frame exists. It commits the applet's record, and a commit writes the complete capability set: every capability in kehto's `ALL_CAPABILITIES` is granted when `BASELINE_DOMAINS` or an allowed domain needs it and revoked otherwise, then the blocked flag is applied and the ACL persisted. The permissive default is never consulted for an applet kernl runs, because every capability has an entry.
2. **Environment narrowing.** `createEnvironmentResolver(grants)` is the `ShellAdapter.capabilities.resolveEnvironment` hook. For each identity it returns the baseline plus the domains the user allowed, intersected with what the shell offers live; a blocked applet gets `shell` alone, enough to finish the handshake and nothing more. kehto intersects the result with its own availability set, so the hook can only remove. The applet's `shell.init` therefore advertises a subset.
3. **Runtime firewall rules.** `kernl.mount` calls `applyRuntimeFirewallRules`, which translates the guard profile's per-class rates into kehto's runtime firewall through `RUNTIME_OP_CLASSES` so that over-budget envelopes are refused before dispatch. It sets no policy: kehto's `allow` policy would skip every check, and deny and block are the grants layer's job. The one policy kernl writes there is the momentary `deny` of `refuseCurrentDispatch`, which refuses a single oversized envelope. [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#where-enforcement-happens) has the translation table.

The baseline is `BASELINE_DOMAINS`: `shell`, `inc`, `theme` and `storage`. It has no network, and it is not read-only: the handshake, in-shell messaging, the theme, and the applet's own scoped storage, which it reads and writes within its state quota. Who the user is, is not in it. `identity` is a grant like any other ("your account" in the shell): until the user grants it, the shell does not tell an applet which account is signed in, its public key or its profile (SOUL opinion 2). Other grants can reveal the account indirectly, and the shell does not hide that: an applet granted `relay` that publishes gets the signed event back in `relay.publish.result`, and a signed event carries the author's public key. `grants.revokeDomain` refuses a baseline domain with `denied:baseline-domain`; `grants.allowDomain` refuses a domain the shell does not offer with `invalid:domain`, and is a no-op for a baseline domain.

The practical effect for an applet: `requires` in the manifest is honoured as a question, not a demand. `MountPlan.missingRequired` lists the required domains the environment does not include, and the host decides what to do before mounting; the web shell's launcher shows the required and optional domains as choices and calls `grants.allowDomain` for the ones the user turns on before it calls `kernl.plan`.

## Consent for destructive writes

Most writes an applet asks the shell to sign are additive: a note, a reaction, a comment. Some replace or erase the account's public record, and kernl asks before signing those. The check is kernl's, not kehto's: kehto's runtime has no consent step for destructive signing. `createKernl` builds one gate with `createSigningConsent` (`consent/handler.ts`) and puts both routes an applet's write can take through it:

- **`relay.publish`.** kehto signs through `ShellAdapter.auth.getSigner(windowId)`; the signer kernl returns for a window awaits the gate in `signEvent` before the account signs.
- **`outbox.publish`.** kehto's outbox service signs without naming the window, so kernl gates `outbox.publish` in the service wrapper (`kernl-services.ts`) before the message reaches the service; a refusal is answered as `outbox.publish.result` with `ok: false`.

`isDestructiveKind` accepts every replaceable kind (0, 3, 10000–19999), because signing one overwrites the version before it; every addressable kind (30000–39999), for the same reason; kind 5, a deletion; and kind 62, a request to vanish. For those, the gate first looks up the current version: `lookupReplaceable` reads the `EventStore` and, on a miss, asks the user's outbox and discovery relays through the applesauce address loader, waiting at most `CURRENT_VERSION_TIMEOUT_MS` (4000 ms). It then runs `describeChange(draft, before, applet)` (`consent/describe-change.ts`):

| Kind | Severity | What the user sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | `destructive` | "Update your profile": one line per changed field, with the value before and after. |
| `3` | `destructive` | "Change who you follow": follows added and removed, counted, the first three named by abbreviated key. |
| `5` | `destructive` | "Delete N items", or "Delete N posts" when the `k` tags say every target is a post: one line per event id (`e` tag), and one "Delete every version of" line per address (`a` tag), named in plain words such as `record (type 30001) "books" by person 3bf0c63f…`. |
| `62` | `destructive` | "Ask services to erase your account": everything the account published, and which services are asked. |
| `10002` | `destructive` | "Change your connections list": relays added and removed with their read/write markers. |
| 10000–10099, 30000–30099 | `destructive` | "Change the list …": entries added and removed, each named as a person, item, topic, type, server or key rather than as a raw tag. |
| any other replaceable or addressable kind | `destructive` | "Replace one of your records (type N)": tags added and removed, and "Content: Replaced" when the content changes, without copying it. |
| everything else | `routine` | No prompt; the event is signed without asking. |

When no current version is found, in the store or on the network within the timeout, a replaceable or addressable summary starts with "Current version: could not be loaded; this replaces it entirely" (`UNKNOWN_CURRENT_VERSION`), so the user is not shown a first version that seems to remove nothing.

The gate calls `host.presentConsent({ summary, resolve })` and waits. *Allow* signs the event. Deny or dismiss rejects with `denied:consent`: nothing is signed and nothing is published. The core never times a prompt out. A destructive write from a window kernl did not mount is refused with `denied:unknown-applet`, one while nobody is signed in with `denied:signed-out`, and a write whose kind is not a number with `invalid:event-kind`.

Three limits are deliberate:

- **Only applet windows are gated.** The shell's own signing, which has no window id, goes through the account's signer directly.
- **Answers are not remembered.** Each destructive write asks again; `ConsentPrompt` has no "always allow" switch.
- **The user never approves raw JSON.** The unsigned draft (empty `id` and `sig`) is on `ConsentSummary.event` for an "advanced" disclosure.

kehto's own `ConsentRequest` is a different thing: the runtime raises it, without an event, when a firewall policy is `prompt`. `createConsentHandler` is registered for it and refuses those without asking; a future request that carries an event, from a window the shell can name, would be described and put to the user. kernl sets no runtime policy except the momentary `deny` of `refuseCurrentDispatch`, and never `ask`, so the firewall path is not expected.

Deletions are not rate-limited more tightly than other publishes before dispatch: kind 5 shares the `relay:write` budget in kehto's runtime firewall. The guard's separate `relay:publish:delete` bucket runs only in kernl's own focus firewall, which observes each envelope before dispatch but cannot hold it, so an overrun becomes a guard event ([Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#where-enforcement-happens)).

## What the applet learns

The applet learns its own narrowed environment through `shell.init`. Without the `identity` grant it is not told who is signed in. It does not learn why a domain is missing, whether other applets have it, or what the user's other grants are. The shell never gives it `window.nostr`, a key, the `EventStore`, or plaintext the user did not ask the shell to show it.

## Related

- [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md): the behavioural limits that apply once a grant exists.
- [Grant and revoke](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/grant-and-revoke.md): the shell-side calls.
- [Security posture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/security-posture.md): the mount rules this page relies on.

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/layouts.md -->

# Layouts

`@kehto/wm` ships only a contract: a `LayoutStrategy` is a pure `arrange(windows, containerRect)` that returns one `WindowPlacement` (`{ id, rect }`) per window it places. Each `WindowState` it receives has an `id`, `focused`, `minimized` and a `rect` of `{ x, y, w, h }`. kehto leaves the strategies to the shell. `@kernl/core` supplies four in `packages/core/src/wm/layouts.ts`, and the shell app uses tiling of its own, described at the end of this page.

## The four strategies

| Export | Kind | Arrangement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `floatingLayout` | constant | Every window keeps the rectangle it has, copied. Minimised windows are returned too, unchanged. |
| `createDwindleLayout(options?)` | factory | Each window after the first takes half of the area that is left, splitting into columns, then rows, in turn, so the last window ends in the smallest corner. The last window takes all that remains. |
| `createColumnsLayout(options?)` | factory | Equal-width columns, full height, in window order. |
| `createMasterStackLayout(options?)` | factory | One master window on the left, the rest stacked in equal rows on the right. The focused window is the master; with no focused window, the first is. A single window fills the container. |

The three tiling factories take `LayoutOptions`: `gap`, the pixels between windows and from the container edge, default `0`. `createMasterStackLayout` also takes `ratio`, the master's share of the width after the gap, default `0.6`.

Rules shared by the tiling strategies:

- **Minimised windows are left out.** They get no placement, so the visible windows share the whole container. A strategy given only minimised windows returns an empty list.
- **Rectangles are rounded** to whole pixels.
- **Order is the caller's.** Dwindle and columns place windows in the order they are passed; only master-stack looks at `focused`.

`packages/core/features/layouts.feature` specifies all four.

```ts
import { createMasterStackLayout } from '@kernl/core';

const layout = createMasterStackLayout({ ratio: 0.5, gap: 8 });
const placements = layout.arrange(
  [
    { id: 'notes', focused: false, minimized: false, rect: { x: 0, y: 0, w: 400, h: 300 } },
    { id: 'pulse', focused: true, minimized: false, rect: { x: 0, y: 0, w: 400, h: 300 } },
    { id: 'clock', focused: false, minimized: true, rect: { x: 0, y: 0, w: 400, h: 300 } },
  ],
  { x: 0, y: 0, w: 1200, h: 800 },
);
// pulse is the master at { x: 8, y: 8, w: 588, h: 784 }; notes fills the stack at { x: 604, y: 8, w: 588, h: 784 }; clock is not placed
```

## How the shell lays out windows

The shell app (`apps/web`) does not call the `@kernl/core` strategies. Its window store (`apps/web/src/shell/window-store.svelte.ts`) has two modes, chosen from the bar's layout control and remembered in `kernl:layout:v1` ([Persistence](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/persistence.md)):

| Mode | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `floating` (default) | Each window keeps its own rectangle. New windows cascade from near the top left in 32 px steps, and a moved or resized window, like every window when the desktop resizes, is kept inside the desktop at no less than 280 × 160 px, or the desktop's own size when that is smaller. |
| `tiled` | The shell's own `dwindle(area, count)` in `apps/web/src/shell/layout.ts` places the windows that are neither minimised nor stopped, in opening order, with an 8 px gap between them and none at the desktop edge. It is the same arrangement as `createDwindleLayout`, written against the shell's `{ x, y, width, height }` rectangle. |

At 720 px wide or less the shell is compact: every window fills the desktop, whatever the mode ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#what-does-not-work-yet)).

Minimising matters beyond layout. A minimised window is hidden, and the guard watches a hidden window more closely: its resource requests are counted against the hidden-window allowance, and the visibility gate holds its first window-level message ([Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md)).

An embedding host that renders its own windows can pass any `LayoutStrategy`, including the four above, to whatever arranges them; the core does not hold a layout of its own.

## Related

- [Architecture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md)
- [`@kernl/core`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md)
- [Embed kernl core](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/embed-kernl-core.md)

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/messaging.md -->

# Messaging

No encrypted messaging protocol is inherently superior. Each one trades metadata exposure, forward secrecy and reach against the others, and the right trade depends on who the user is writing to. kernl therefore supports several and ranks none ([D-009](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-009)). A provider describes its own properties truthfully; the shell shows the description and lets the user choose.

In this alpha `private` and `legacy` work in the live shell when the signed-in account's signer can encrypt; `ratchet` needs a runtime that does not ship and is unavailable. The offline preview runs all three over the in-memory backend, and messages sent there go nowhere ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#messaging-providers-in-the-live-shell)).

## The provider contract

A `MessagingProvider` in `@kernl/messaging` is a pluggable module with one contract:

```ts
import type { MessagingBackend, ProviderAvailability, SecurityProperties } from '@kernl/messaging';

interface MessagingProvider {
  readonly id: string;              // conversation-id prefix: 'private', 'legacy', 'ratchet'
  readonly name: string;            // user-facing, no protocol vocabulary
  readonly description: string;     // one sentence for the picker
  readonly properties: SecurityProperties;
  availability(): ProviderAvailability;
  createBackend(): MessagingBackend;
}
```

`createBackend()` returns a `MessagingBackend`: `status`, `conversations`, `messages`, `send`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe` and an optional `close`. The shape is structurally identical to kehto's `DmAdapter`, so a backend can be handed to `createDmService` without translation while this package stays free of a kehto dependency. The wire types (`DmConversation`, `DmMessage`, `DmSendRequest` and friends) come from `@napplet/core`. Every method except `send` may return a value or a promise.

The package holds no relay code, signer or store. A provider is built with `defineProvider(definition, deps)`, where `definition` is the fixed, user-facing part (`id`, `name`, `description`, `properties`) and `deps` is what the shell injects:

```ts
import type { MessagingBackend, ProviderAvailability } from '@kernl/messaging';

interface ProviderDeps {
  createBackend: () => MessagingBackend;     // called once per enable; the registry owns the instance
  available: () => ProviderAvailability;     // { available: true } or { available: false, reason }
}
```

The three built-in factories (`createPrivateMessagesProvider`, `createLegacyMessagesProvider`, `createRatchetMessagesProvider`) take the same `ProviderDeps` and supply the definition themselves. In the shell, `@kernl/core` builds each provider's `ProviderDeps`: `createKernl` supplies `createPrivateMessagesBackend` and `createLegacyMessagesBackend` unless `KernlOptions.messagingBackends` overrides them, and `available` follows the active account ([The shell's backends](#the-shell-s-backends)). In tests and the preview, `createBackend` returns `createMemoryBackend()`. See `providers.feature`, scenario "availability and the backend come from the shell".

## Security properties

`SecurityProperties` is a fixed set of fields. Every field except `specification` is required, and the shell renders them verbatim with no summary score:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `forwardSecrecy` | Compromise of today's keys does not reveal yesterday's messages. |
| `postCompromiseSecurity` | The session heals after a compromise once both parties exchange messages. |
| `metadataProtection` | `none`, `partial` or `strong`: how much a network observer learns about who talks to whom and when. |
| `requiresSameClient` | The correspondent must use a client that speaks this provider. |
| `groups` | Conversations with more than two participants are supported. |
| `specification` | Optional. Where the protocol is specified. Shown in these docs, not in the public UI. |
| `experimental` | The provider is still changing and may lose history between versions. |

`describeProvider(provider)` turns them into the six rows the picker shows, in this order and with these labels: `Forward secrecy`, `Recovers after a key compromise`, `Metadata protection`, `Correspondent needs the same app`, `Group conversations`, `Experimental`. Booleans render as `yes`/`no`; `metadataProtection` renders as is; `specification` is left out so no protocol name reaches the UI ([D-006](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-006)).

## The three providers

| Provider id | Name | `specification` | What the specification is | Forward secrecy | Post-compromise security | Metadata protection | Same client required | Groups | Experimental |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `private` | Private messages | `'NIP-17'` | Gift-wrapped private messages: kind 14 rumours sealed in kind 13, wrapped in kind 1059 with a random key | no | no | `partial`: the wrap hides sender and timing from relays, the recipient's inbox relays still see delivery | no | yes | no |
| `legacy` | Legacy messages | `'NIP-04'` | Direct messages: kind 4, shared-secret encryption | no | no | `none`: sender, recipient and timing are public on the event | no | no | no |
| `ratchet` | Ratchet sessions | `'nostr-double-ratchet (draft)'` | A double-ratchet session protocol over nostr, still a draft | yes | yes | `partial`: per-message ephemeral keys hide the long-term identities, relays still see timing | yes | no | yes |

The descriptions the picker shows: `private` "Sealed messages that hide who is talking to whom from the network."; `legacy` "The original direct-message format. Readable by the widest range of apps, but who you talk to is visible on the network."; `ratchet` "Per-session keys that change with every message. Both sides need an app that supports it."

Three things the table says that the picker says too:

- `legacy` is marked as metadata-exposing because it is. It exists because many correspondents can read nothing else, and the user is told that before choosing it.
- `private` has no forward secrecy. A gift wrap protects metadata, not past messages, and the picker does not claim otherwise.
- `private` and `legacy` are available only while the active account's signer can encrypt: `nip44` for `private`, `nip04` for `legacy`. Otherwise kernl reports `sign-in-required` (nobody is signed in) or `signer-cannot-encrypt` (a read-only account, or a signer without the method).
- `ratchet` is available only when the shell's `available()` says so. The package does not decide the reason; kernl's `createDefaultMessaging` supplies `no-runtime` (`MESSAGING_UNAVAILABLE_REASONS.noRuntime`), `enable()` rethrows it as `unavailable:no-runtime`, and `list()` reports it so the picker can show the provider greyed with that reason. Its specification is a draft and the provider is flagged `experimental`.

## The shell's backends

`@kernl/core` ships the two network backends the live shell uses ([D-015](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-015)). Both take the shell's one `EventStore`, `RelayPool` and relay tiers, and read the signer and the user's public key through functions, so they follow the active account without being rebuilt:

- **`createPrivateMessagesBackend`** sends NIP-17 messages. The message is an unsigned kind 14 rumour; it is sealed in a kind 13 event that the account signer signs, encrypting with its `nip44`; the seal is wrapped in a kind 1059 event signed by a one-time key. That key is generated inside an applesauce `PrivateKeySigner`, used for one wrap and discarded; it is never stored. The wrap goes to the recipient's kind 10050 inbox relays, or to the sender's `outbox` and `super` tiers when the recipient publishes none, and a second wrap goes to the sender so their other devices see the message. The backend subscribes to kind 1059 events tagged with the user's public key on the user's own inbox relays, or the same tiers. A conversation id is applesauce's `createConversationIdentifier`: the participants' public keys, the user's included, sorted and joined by `:`, so both sides compute the same id. Decrypted messages are kept in memory per account, never in the `EventStore`, and are cleared when the account changes or signs out; the `EventStore` is read only for inbox relay lists.
- **`createLegacyMessagesBackend`** sends NIP-04 kind 4 messages through `signer.nip04`, with the same conversation ids and message shape. It is the metadata-exposing provider: who writes to whom, and when, is public on the event.

Neither backend touches key bytes. Everything is signed and encrypted by the account's applesauce signer; an extension or remote signer may ask its own question per decryption, and kernl lets it.

The Messages panel opens the user's own messages without a consent prompt from kernl: the shell is asking, for the user, to show the user their own mail. Applets are different. An applet reaches messages only through the NAP `dm` domain, which is a grant the user gives per applet and can revoke ([Identity and grants](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md)).

## The registry

The shell holds exactly one `MessagingRegistry`, built with `createMessagingRegistry({ preferences?, onChange? })`. It owns the backend instances:

- `register(provider)` adds a provider. Nothing is enabled by registration unless the saved `preferences.enabled` list names the provider; then it is enabled at once if available, and left disabled (reporting why through `list()`) if not. A second registration of the same id throws `invalid:duplicate-provider`.
- `enable(id)` calls `availability()` and throws `unavailable:<reason>` when the provider cannot run; otherwise it calls `createBackend()` once and keeps the instance. Enabling an enabled provider does nothing. Unknown ids throw `invalid:unknown-provider`.
- `disable(id)` calls the backend's `close?()` and drops it. If the default pointed at it, the default is cleared.
- `setDefault(id)` names the provider for sends that name no provider and no conversation. The provider must be enabled, else `invalid:provider-not-enabled`. A saved `defaultProvider` is restored when that provider registers, unless `setDefault` was called first.
- `preferences()` returns a frozen `{ enabled, defaultProvider? }` snapshot; `onChange` receives the same snapshot after every change.
- `composite()` returns one `MessagingBackend` spanning every enabled provider, for the NAP `dm` service. It is the same instance on every call and sees providers come and go.
- `close()` closes every backend and leaves the preferences untouched, so a shutdown never erases what the user chose. A closed registry is not reused.

See `registry.feature`, scenarios "saved preferences enable providers as they register" and "closing the registry closes every backend and keeps the preferences".

## The composite backend

The NAP `dm` domain is a projection over every enabled provider. `createCompositeBackend(resolveEnabled, getDefault)` builds it, and the only thing an applet can observe is the id namespace:

- Every conversation and message id leaving the composite is `"<providerId>:<innerId>"`, built by `namespaceId`. `private:direct:ab,cd` is the conversation `direct:ab,cd` as the `private` provider knows it. The inner id may itself contain `:`; `splitId` splits on the first one only.
- Ids arriving from the applet are split to find the provider. An id without a prefix, or with a prefix no enabled provider owns, rejects with `invalid:unknown-provider`.
- `conversations()` with a cursor routes to the provider named in the cursor and passes the inner cursor through. Without a cursor and with exactly one provider enabled, the provider's page is returned with its cursor namespaced (`private:2`). With several providers, every provider's page is fetched, the conversations are merged and sorted by `updatedAt` descending (conversations without activity sort last), `limit` is applied to the merged list, and the page carries no cursor, because no single provider can resume a merged page.
- `messages()` routes by the conversation prefix and prefixes the ids on the way out.
- `send()` routes by the conversation id when there is one, else by the `provider` field (`WithProvider<DmSendRequest>`) the shell adds when the user picks a provider for a new conversation, else by the default provider. An unknown provider rejects with `invalid:unknown-provider`; no default, or a default that is no longer enabled, rejects with `unavailable:no-default-provider`.
- `subscribe()` with a conversation id subscribes on that provider; without one it subscribes on every enabled provider and fans the messages in, prefixed. Subscription ids are `composite-<n>`. Unsubscribing skips providers disabled in the meantime, since disabling already closed their backend, and reports `ok: false` if any surviving provider did.
- `status()` merges: `available` if any provider is, the first `ownerPubkey` found, the union of `implementations` and `capabilities`.
- `close()` on the composite is a no-op. The registry owns backend lifetimes.

An applet that uses `dm` therefore sees one inbox. Which provider carries a given conversation is visible in its id, and the shell shows it as a label the user can change for new conversations. See `composite.feature`.

## The in-memory backend

`createMemoryBackend({ owner?, available?, now? })` is a complete `MessagingBackend` with no network, used by the shell's offline preview and by every feature in this package. Conversations are keyed `direct:<pubkey>` or `group:<pubkey>,<pubkey>` over the sorted correspondents with the owner removed; `send()` stores the message as `sent` (id `msg-<n>`, or the request's `clientMessageId`) and notifies subscribers; `deliver({ senderPubkey, content, conversationId?, createdAt? })` plays the other side and stores a `received` message; unread counts are the number of `received` messages; cursors are numeric offsets with default page sizes of 50 conversations and 100 messages. `send()` rejects with `invalid:no-recipients`, `invalid:unknown-conversation` or `unavailable:offline`; reads keep working offline so a preview can still show history. See `memory-backend.feature`.

## Error reasons

| Reason | Thrown by |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid:duplicate-provider` | `register` |
| `invalid:unknown-provider` | `enable`, `disable` (unknown id); composite routing of ids, cursors and `provider` hints |
| `unavailable:<reason>` | `enable` when `availability()` is false; `<reason>` is the shell's word |
| `invalid:provider-not-enabled` | `setDefault` |
| `unavailable:no-default-provider` | composite `send` with no conversation, no hint and no usable default |
| `invalid:no-recipients`, `invalid:unknown-conversation`, `unavailable:offline` | memory backend `send` |

## Related

- [Add a messaging provider](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/add-a-messaging-provider.md)
- [`@kernl/messaging`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/messaging.md)

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/persistence.md -->

# Persistence

kernl keeps the user's choices in the browser they made them in, and nowhere else. There is no kernl server, no sync and no account to log in to. This page lists every key kernl writes, what each holds, and what is deliberately never written.

## Where values go

`@kernl/core` never touches `localStorage` itself. It writes to `KernlHost.storage`, a `StorageLike` (`getItem`, `setItem`, `removeItem`) the host supplies. The shell app supplies `pickStorage()` from `apps/web/src/shell/host.ts`: `localStorage` when a probe write succeeds, otherwise a `Map` that lives as long as the page. In a private window that refuses storage, the shell still works and forgets everything on reload.

Inside the core, every key goes through `createNamespacedStore(storage, 'kernl')`, which prefixes each key with `kernl:` and stores JSON:

| Method | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `getJson(key, fallback)` | Reads `kernl:<key>` and parses it. Returns `fallback` when the key is absent or the JSON is corrupt; it never throws, so a damaged value cannot stop the shell from booting. |
| `setJson(key, value)` | Serialises and writes `kernl:<key>`. |
| `remove(key)` | Removes `kernl:<key>`. |

The prefix keeps kernl's keys apart from kehto's and from the host app's in the same storage. Every key carries a `:v1` suffix so a future format can move to `:v2` without reading the old one wrongly.

## Keys the core writes

| Key | Written by | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kernl:accounts:v1` | `createKernlAccounts` | applesauce's `AccountManager.toJSON(true)`: the serialised accounts, minus any that cannot be serialised. Rewritten whenever the account list changes. |
| `kernl:active-account:v1` | `createKernlAccounts` | The active account's id. Removed when no account is active. |
| `kernl:grants:v1` | `createGrants` | One record per verified applet build, keyed `<dTag>:<hash>`: `{ dTag, hash, domains, blocked }`. See [Identity and grants](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md). |
| `kernl:relays:v1` | `createRelayTiers` | The four relay tiers, each a list of URLs. See [Relay tiers](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/relay-tiers.md). |
| `kernl:messaging:v1` | `createDefaultMessaging` | `MessagingPreferences`: the `enabled` provider ids and the optional `defaultProvider`. See [Messaging](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/messaging.md). |

On boot, `createKernlAccounts` restores the accounts and makes the stored id active if that account still exists. `createGrants` loads its records, and `createRelayTiers` and `createDefaultMessaging` start from the stored value when there is one.

## Keys the shell app writes

| Key | Written by | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kernl:recent:v1` | `recent.ts`, through the host storage | The recently opened applets: up to eight `{ address, title, publisher, openedAt }`, newest first. Opening an applet moves it to the front; the launcher can forget one. |
| `kernl:layout:v1` | `window-store.svelte.ts`, to `localStorage` directly | `floating` or `tiled`, as a plain string. A refused write is ignored and the layout applies to the current page only. See [Layouts](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/layouts.md). |
| `kernl:preview:grants:v1`, `kernl:preview:relays:v1`, `kernl:preview:messaging:v1` | the offline preview (`?preview=1`) | The preview's own grants, tiers and messaging preferences, kept apart so that trying the preview never changes the live shell's state. |

The public website also remembers its colour scheme as `kernl-theme` (`light` or `dark`). That key belongs to the site pages, not to the shell.

## Keys kehto writes

kernl passes no persistence hooks of its own to `createShellBridge`, so kehto uses its defaults from `@kehto/shell`, which write to `localStorage` directly rather than to `host.storage`. In `@kehto/shell` 0.29.0 those are `napplet:acl` (the runtime ACL, which `kernl:grants:v1` mirrors per applet build), `napplet:manifest-cache`, `napplet-shell-secret`, `napplet-guid:<windowId>`, and the scoped keys behind the `storage` NAP domain, where an applet's own data lives. kernl does not read or migrate these keys; their format is kehto's.

## What is never persisted

- **Plaintext private keys.** `KernlAccountManager.addAccount` refuses the account types whose serialised form carries a raw secret (`PLAINTEXT_KEY_ACCOUNT_TYPES`: `nsec` and `seed-words`) with `denied:plaintext-key-persistence`, and restore drops any such entry it finds in storage. The only stored form of a local key is applesauce's `PasswordAccount`, whose `ncryptsec` is NIP-49 encrypted with the user's password. The password itself is never stored.
- **The preview account.** "Try the preview" creates a throwaway key account in a plain `AccountManager` that is not connected to storage, so it disappears on reload.
- **The guard profile.** `GuardFacade.setProfile` changes the profile for the running shell only. Every boot starts `strict` ([D-003](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-003)).
- **Open windows.** The window store persists only the layout. Applets are not reopened on reload; the recent list is how the user gets back to them.

Some stored values are sensitive even though they are not the user's key. A browser-extension account stores only its public key, because the extension holds the secret. A remote-signer account stores what applesauce needs to reconnect: the remote signer's public key, its relays, the pairing secret when there is one, and the client key of the pairing session in hex. That client key is not the user's identity key, but anyone who reads it from this browser's storage can talk to the remote signer as this session until the user revokes the pairing in the signer.

## Clearing it

Signing out clears the active account and keeps the account in the list, so it can be picked again. **Forget** on the sign-in screen removes a stored account. Removing everything kernl stored means clearing the site's storage in the browser. Nothing is held anywhere else, so there is nothing else to delete.

## Related

- [Identity and grants](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/identity-and-grants.md)
- [Relay tiers](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/relay-tiers.md)
- [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#what-does-not-work-yet)

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/relay-tiers.md -->

# Relay tiers

The shell, not the applet, decides which relays a request goes to. It sorts its relays into four tiers, routes each request to one tier by the kinds it asks for, and lets the user edit every tier in Settings. Applets never name a relay for an ordinary query or publish; the one exception is a scoped relay a window opens for itself, described at the end of this page.

## The four tiers

kehto's `RelayConfigHooks` knows three tiers: `discovery`, `super` and `outbox`. kernl adds a fourth, `apps`, for applet manifests. The `RelayTier` type is the union of the four names.

| Tier | Settings label | What it serves | Default relays (`DEFAULT_RELAY_TIERS`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `discovery` | Discovery | Profiles, follow lists and relay lists (kinds `0`, `3`, `10002`) | `wss://purplepag.es`, `wss://relay.nos.social` |
| `apps` | Applet catalogue | Applet manifests (kehto's `NAPPLET_KINDS`, `5129`, `15129` and `35129`, plus the legacy catalogue kind `32267`) | `wss://relay.napplet.soy` |
| `outbox` | Your connections | Where what the user publishes is delivered | none |
| `super` | General | Everything that is not discovery or manifests | `wss://relay.damus.io`, `wss://nos.lol`, `wss://relay.primal.net` |

`DEFAULT_RELAY_TIERS` is exported from `@kernl/core` as a frozen `TierMap`, each tier a frozen array. The outbox tier starts empty: kernl does not guess where the user publishes.

## How a request picks a tier

`selectRelayTier(tiers, filters)` in `packages/core/src/applesauce/relay-hooks.ts` collects the kinds of every filter and chooses:

1. If any filter has no `kinds`, or an empty `kinds`, the request cannot be classified and takes the general path.
2. If every kind is `0`, `3` or `10002`, the request goes to the `discovery` tier.
3. If every kind is an applet-manifest kind, the request goes to the `apps` tier.
4. Otherwise it goes to `super` and `outbox` together.

The result is deduplicated. A request that mixes a profile kind and a note kind is not split; it takes the general path as a whole.

<!-- sample:skip illustrative calls; the tiers object comes from createKernl or createRelayTiers -->
```ts
selectRelayTier(tiers, [{ kinds: [0], authors: [pubkey] }]); // tiers.get().discovery
selectRelayTier(tiers, [{ kinds: [35129] }]);                 // tiers.get().apps
selectRelayTier(tiers, [{ kinds: [1] }]);                     // super, then outbox
selectRelayTier(tiers, [{ ids: [id] }]);                      // super, then outbox: no kinds
```

The same function is used everywhere the shell picks relays on its own:

- kehto's relay service asks `RelayPoolHooks.selectRelayTier`, which `createRelayPoolHooks` answers with this function.
- kernl's applesauce relay backend (`relay-backend.ts`) uses it for a subscription or query that names no relays, and for every publish, by the published event's kind. A published profile therefore goes to the discovery tier, and a published note to `super` plus `outbox`.
- Manifest lookups (`fetchManifestEvent`) ask the relays named in the applet's address plus the whole `apps` tier.
- The destructive-write consent lookup, which fetches the current version of a replaceable event before the user is asked, asks `outbox` plus `discovery`.

## Where the configuration lives

`createRelayTiers(storage, defaults?)` builds the configuration and returns a `RelayTiers`: `get()`, `add(tier, url)`, `remove(tier, url)` and `changes$`. `createKernl` calls it with `host.storage` and `KernlOptions.relays`, and exposes it as `kernl.relays`.

- **Persistence key.** The whole map is written as JSON to `kernl:relays:v1` (the key `relays:v1` in a `createNamespacedStore` with prefix `kernl`) on every change. See [Persistence](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/persistence.md).
- **Start-up.** When `kernl:relays:v1` holds a value, each tier it names replaces the default for that tier and any tier it lacks keeps `DEFAULT_RELAY_TIERS`. The host's `KernlOptions.relays` is applied over the defaults only when nothing is persisted, so once the user has edited a tier, the host's overrides no longer apply on that device. A corrupt value reads as absent.
- **Validation.** `add` accepts only `ws://` or `wss://` followed by non-space characters and throws `invalid:relay-url` for anything else. Adding a URL a tier already holds does nothing. `remove` of a URL the tier does not hold does nothing.
- **Observation.** `changes$` is an RxJS `BehaviorSubject`, so a new subscriber receives the current map at once. Every value it emits is frozen.

## How Settings edits them

The shell's Settings panel (`apps/web/src/shell/SettingsPanel.svelte`) has a Network section with one block per tier, labelled as in the table above. It subscribes to `kernl.relays.changes$`, lists each server by name with a Remove button that calls `kernl.relays.remove`, and has a "Server address" field that calls `kernl.relays.add`. A bare hostname is given the secure scheme before it is added (`serverAddress` in `servers.ts`), so typing `relay.example` stores `wss://relay.example`. When `add` throws an `invalid:` reason the panel asks for a server address; any other failure says the server could not be added.

The panel never shows the word relay or a protocol scheme to the user ([Public vocabulary](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/public-vocabulary.md)). A change takes effect for the next request; subscriptions already open keep the relays they were opened with.

The offline preview keeps its own tier state at `kernl:preview:relays:v1`, so editing tiers in the preview never changes the live shell's.

## Scoped relays

kehto lets a window open one relay of its own choosing, the NIP-29 group pattern. `createRelayPoolHooks` keeps this minimal: one open subscription per window, replaced when the window opens another, closed with the window, and events delivered to that window's port only. Publishing to the scoped relay goes to that one relay. Tiers do not apply to scoped relays.

## Related

- [Architecture](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/architecture.md)
- [Persistence](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/persistence.md)
- [`@kernl/core`](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/core.md)
