<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/roadmap.md -->

# Roadmap

Ordered by the tie-breakers in `SOUL.md`: the user's safety and agency first, protocol conformance second, the applet developer's ability to build third. Nothing here is dated. An item moves off this page when its scenarios pass and its docs exist.

## 1. Upstream pull requests to kehto

Filed as [kehto/web #397](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/397), [#398](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/398), [#399](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/399) and [#400](https://github.com/kehto/web/issues/400). Each item shrinks kernl when it lands; see [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#upstream-gaps).

- Forward `getFocusContext`, `onFirewallEvent` and `firewallPersistence` through `ShellAdapter` so the runtime's own firewall can be focus-aware without a second engine in front of it.
- Let the host choose the ACL default policy in `createRuntime`, so a restrictive shell does not have to write every capability explicitly.
- Offer a hook that can hold or drop port traffic, so the visibility gate can hold a hidden applet's envelopes instead of only observing them before dispatch.
- Release `experimental.nestedContextLock` in `@kehto/shell`, so kernl can pass the flag to `prepareNappletSrcdoc` and delete its port of the lock ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)).
- Let the runtime firewall measure envelopes without an `event`, so its size matchers see downloads and queries and kernl can drop `refuseCurrentDispatch` ([D-012](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-012)).
- Expose a setter for the runtime firewall's `unfocusedMultiplier`. Together with the forwarded `getFocusContext`, it lets the runtime refuse an unfocused window at the profile's tightened budget instead of treating every window as focused.

## 2. Bridge backends

Today the torrent, NZB, Soulseek and mail bridges hand the locator to an app on the user's device ([Bridges](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/bridges.md#hand-off-backends)). An in-shell backend replaces the hand-off for its bridge and plugs into the path the HTTP bridge already exercises end to end. In-shell transfers would put the traffic under the shell's grants, guard and revocation, and would also make it the shell's to expose, so each needs its exposure description checked. Order reflects how much of the user's exposure each one changes.

| Backend | Interface | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mail | `MailBackend` | Opens or creates a conversation for a `mailto:` locator inside the shell. Candidate for a shell-side IMAP/JMAP client. Today the device's mail program opens. |
| NZB | `NzbBackend` | Hands an `nzb:` locator to a configured downloader the shell can query. The downloader runs outside the browser; the bridge reports job state. Today the `https` document URL opens on the device. |
| Torrent | `TorrentBackend` | Adds an info hash with its trackers. WebTorrent in the shell, or a configured external client the shell can query. Marked as public activity in the exposure description. Today the magnet link opens on the device. |
| Soulseek | `SoulseekBackend` | Requests one file from one peer. Requires a daemon; the bridge reports job state. Today the `slsk://` address opens on the device. |

The shell also needs a downloads view that shows the state of each `job` result and lets the user cancel it; there is none today. A hand-off job cannot be tracked at all, because the transfer belongs to the device app.

## 3. Messaging

- Supply the double-ratchet runtime so the `ratchet` provider reports `available`. Its properties are already described; see [Messaging](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/messaging.md).
- Inbox setup: offer to publish the user's kind 10050 inbox relays when they have none, so `private` stops falling back to the `outbox` and `super` tiers ([D-015](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-015)).
- Per-conversation provider migration: move a correspondent from `legacy` to `private` when both clients can read it, shown as a reversible choice.

## 4. Mobile layouts

The window manager contracts come from `@kehto/wm`. A narrow-viewport layout with a window switcher, gestures for focus and dismissal, and the same visibility semantics the guard relies on (a window off screen is hidden, and hidden windows are deferred).

## 5. Account switching

`AccountManager` already holds several accounts. The missing piece is a switcher that makes the active account visible on every screen, keeps grants scoped to the account that gave them, and never signs a write with an account the user did not pick for that window.

## 6. Guard

- Per-applet guard profiles: today the profile is shell-wide and resets to `strict` on boot ([D-003](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-003)). Next: an override per applet identity, remembered locally.
- Re-narrow a live applet's advertised environment when a domain is revoked; today the ACL denies at once but `shell.init` only changes on the next open.
- Bridge consent per host: wire `createDefaultBridges({ authorize })` to a host prompt so a granted `resource` request still asks before reaching a new origin.
- Persist per-applet profile overrides and grants through a user-chosen sync, so loosening an applet once does not have to be repeated per device.

## 7. Conformance

- Run `@napplet/conformance` against the shell's bridge in `pnpm test`: envelope validators per NAP domain, manifest validation and the reference mock shell's expectations of a host. Today conformance is checked by the `packages/*/features/` scenarios and review only ([Spec conformance](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/policies/spec-conformance.md)).

## Not planned

- A flag in the hosted shell that turns a mitigation off or loosens it for every applet without the user. `SOUL.md` opinion three rules it out. `KernlOptions.guard.profile` lets an embedding host pick the starting limits only.
- A second event library beside applesauce. `DECISIONS.md` [D-002](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-002) rules it out.
- A "recommended" messaging provider. [D-009](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-009) rules it out.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/embed-a-host-page.md -->

# Embed kernl in a page

This tutorial builds the smallest page that runs a real applet under kernl: one HTML file, one script, an address field and a frame. By the end you will have resolved a published applet, verified its code, mounted it in a sandboxed frame you own, and watched the guard report on it. It takes about twenty minutes.

[Embed kernl core](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/embed-kernl-core.md) is the reference version of the same work; this page goes one step at a time and tells you what you should see after each.

> **Alpha**
>
> The `@kernl/*` packages are not on npm yet. You need a clone of the kernl source repository, which is private during the alpha ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)).

## 1. Make a workspace package

In your clone, build the packages once, then create a package for your page under `apps/`, which `pnpm-workspace.yaml` already covers:

```bash
pnpm install && pnpm build
mkdir -p apps/my-host/src && cd apps/my-host
```

Give it a `package.json` that depends on the core and the account library through the workspace, and on Vite as a dev server. Any bundler that resolves workspace packages works; Vite is the shortest path.

```json
{
  "name": "my-host",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": { "dev": "vite" },
  "dependencies": {
    "@kernl/core": "workspace:^",
    "@kernl/guard": "workspace:^",
    "applesauce-accounts": "^7.0.2"
  },
  "devDependencies": { "vite": "^7.0.0" }
}
```

Run `pnpm install` from the repository root.

**Checkpoint.** `apps/my-host/node_modules/@kernl/core` is a link to `packages/core`, and `packages/core/dist/index.js` exists. If `dist/` is missing, run `pnpm build` at the root again.

## 2. Write the page

Create `apps/my-host/index.html`. The `<meta>` in the head is kernl's frame policy (`KERNL_FRAME_POLICY_META`): it stops applet frames from loading or navigating to any URL, so their only content is the verified `srcdoc` kernl assigns. It has to be in the HTML the server sends, before any script runs.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-src 'none'">
    <title>My kernl host</title>
    <style>
      body { font: 16px system-ui, sans-serif; margin: 2rem; }
      #frames iframe { width: 100%; height: 480px; border: 1px solid #888; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body>
    <form id="open">
      <label>Account id (public key, read-only) <input name="pubkey" size="64" /></label>
      <label>Applet address <input name="address" size="64" /></label>
      <button>Open</button>
    </form>
    <p id="status">Not started.</p>
    <div id="frames"></div>
    <pre id="events"></pre>
    <script type="module" src="/src/main.ts"></script>
  </body>
</html>
```

**Checkpoint.** `pnpm dev` in `apps/my-host` serves the form at the URL Vite prints. The status line reads "Not started."; the script does not exist yet, so the browser console shows a 404 for `main.ts`.

## 3. Implement the host

Create `apps/my-host/src/main.ts`. The core never touches the page directly; everything it needs from the page goes through a `KernlHost`. This one stores in `localStorage`, asks with `window.confirm`, and reports visibility from the document.

```ts
import { createKernl, type ConsentPrompt, type KernlHost } from '@kernl/core';
import type { WindowVisibility } from '@kernl/guard';

const status = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#status')!;
const frames = new Map<string, HTMLIFrameElement>();

function visibilityOf(windowId: string): WindowVisibility {
  const visible = frames.has(windowId) && document.visibilityState === 'visible';
  return { visible, focused: visible && document.hasFocus() };
}

function describe(prompt: ConsentPrompt): string {
  const lines = prompt.summary.lines.map((line) => `${line.label}: ${line.before ?? '-'} -> ${line.after ?? '-'}`);
  return [prompt.summary.title, ...lines].join('\n');
}

const host: KernlHost = {
  storage: localStorage,
  presentConsent: (prompt) => prompt.resolve(window.confirm(describe(prompt))),
  notify: (notice) => {
    status.textContent = `${notice.title}${notice.body ? `: ${notice.body}` : ''}`;
  },
  openLink: (url) => void window.open(url, '_blank', 'noopener,noreferrer'),
  getVisibility: visibilityOf,
  onRevoked(windowId, reason) {
    frames.get(windowId)?.remove();
    frames.delete(windowId);
    status.textContent = `The applet was stopped (${reason}).`;
  },
};

const kernl = createKernl({ host });
window.addEventListener('message', (event) => kernl.handleWindowMessage(event));
status.textContent = `Shell ready. Guard profile: ${kernl.guard.config.profile}.`;
```

`createKernl` creates the event store, the connection pool, the account manager, the guard in its `strict` profile and kehto's shell bridge. The `message` listener is how an applet's first message reaches the guard and then the bridge; add it exactly once.

**Checkpoint.** Reload the page. The status line reads "Shell ready. Guard profile: strict." and the console has no errors.

## 4. Sign in read-only

Applets you grant *your account* (`identity`) can see who is at the keyboard. A read-only account is the simplest way to have one: it needs only a public key, and every write an applet asks for is refused because there is no signer. Add to `main.ts`:

<!-- sample:continues -->
```ts
import { ReadonlyAccount } from 'applesauce-accounts/accounts';

async function signIn(pubkey: string): Promise<void> {
  if (kernl.session?.pubkey === pubkey) return;
  const session = await kernl.login(ReadonlyAccount.fromPubkey(pubkey));
  status.textContent = `Signed in as ${session.label} (read-only: ${session.readOnly}).`;
}
```

**Checkpoint.** Nothing changes yet; the function is called in the next step.

## 5. Resolve, plan and mount

This is the whole applet lifecycle: turn the address into a pointer, fetch and verify the applet, record grants, plan the mount, attach an empty frame and hand it to kernl. Add to `main.ts`:

<!-- sample:continues -->
```ts
const form = document.querySelector<HTMLFormElement>('#open')!;
const container = document.querySelector<HTMLDivElement>('#frames')!;

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const data = new FormData(form);
  void open(String(data.get('pubkey') ?? '').trim(), String(data.get('address') ?? '').trim());
});

async function open(pubkey: string, address: string): Promise<void> {
  try {
    if (pubkey) await signIn(pubkey);
    status.textContent = 'Looking up the applet…';
    const summary = await kernl.resolve(kernl.decodePointer(address));
    status.textContent = `Verified "${summary.title}" (build ${summary.identity.hash.slice(0, 8)}).`;

    const plan = await kernl.plan(summary);
    if (plan.missingRequired.length > 0) status.textContent += ` Runs without: ${plan.missingRequired.join(', ')}.`;

    const frame = document.createElement('iframe');
    frame.title = summary.title;
    container.append(frame); // attached and empty: mount needs its contentWindow
    frames.set(plan.windowId, frame);
    const handle = kernl.mount(plan, frame);
    handle.status$.subscribe((state) => {
      if (state === 'running') status.textContent = `"${summary.title}" is running in ${plan.windowId}.`;
    });
  } catch (error) {
    status.textContent = `Could not open it: ${(error as Error).message}`;
  }
}
```

`resolve` verifies the manifest's signature and hashes the applet's code before anything runs; a failure is a stable reason such as `invalid:pointer` or `unavailable:manifest` ([Error reasons](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/reference/errors.md)). `plan` writes the applet's grants explicitly, so it sees only the baseline domains until you allow more. `mount` sets the frame's `sandbox` attribute to exactly `allow-scripts`, registers the window, and only then assigns the verified `srcdoc`. Do not set `src`, `sandbox` or `srcdoc` yourself.

**Checkpoint.** Paste any public key (64 hex characters) and an applet address, then click **Open**. The address below is a puzzle game published by a third party on napplet.run, not by kernl; it needs no grants:

```
naddr1qvzqqqyf8ypzqw49s9e88sajl985jxzquprj7pyapugqp83rme3sqctxhj5mxm4rqythwumn8ghj7un9d3shjtnwv9c8qmr9wsh8xmmeqqxkuttzvy6nyefnxpjr2e3jqg5uk8
```

You should see "Signed in as …", then "Looking up the applet…", then `Verified "Freeze Frame Response" (build b5633add)`, and finally `"Freeze Frame Response" is running in applet-1.` with the game in the frame. The build prefix changes if the publisher releases a new version. "Could not open it: unavailable:manifest" means no connection returned the applet's description; check your network and try again.

## 6. Watch the guard

The guard reports what it notices about each applet as events. Add to `main.ts`:

<!-- sample:continues -->
```ts
const log = document.querySelector<HTMLPreElement>('#events')!;

kernl.guard.events$.subscribe((event) => {
  log.textContent += `${new Date(event.at).toLocaleTimeString()} ${event.windowId} ${event.disposition} ${event.reason}\n`;
});
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  for (const handle of kernl.applets()) handle.setVisibility(visibilityOf(handle.windowId));
});
```

**Checkpoint.** A quiet applet produces no events, so the log stays empty while you play. Switch to another tab and back: the guard now knows the window was hidden, and a hidden applet that keeps downloading past its allowance would be quarantined and reported as `flood:hidden-resource`. What each reason means is in [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#dispositions-and-reasons).

## What you built

A page that is a complete kernl host: it verifies an applet before running it, runs it in a frame with no network of its own, keeps the guard informed, and stops the applet when the guard quarantines it. Two things this page leaves out on purpose:

- **Signing.** A read-only account cannot sign, so the consent prompt never appears. With a signing account, an applet that tries to change your profile, follows, connections or lists, or to delete something, reaches `presentConsent` first, and a "no" fails the write with `denied:consent`.
- **Grants.** The page never calls `kernl.grants.allowDomain`, so applets get only the baseline (`shell`, `inc`, `theme`, `storage`) and are not told who is signed in. [Grant and revoke](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/grant-and-revoke.md) shows the calls.

## Where next

- [Embed kernl core](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/embed-kernl-core.md): the same host with grants and focus tracking.
- [Run the shell](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/run-the-shell.md): the full shell in `apps/web`.
- [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md): what the guard expects of an applet.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/run-the-shell.md -->

# Run the shell

This tutorial takes you from nothing to an applet running in a window, signed in with your own account, and shows the `Kernl` calls behind each step. The hosted preview takes a minute and needs no install; running the shell from source takes about ten minutes and needs access to the source repository.

> **Alpha**
>
> The shell runs, but it is a first draft. Expect rough edges in the UI and read [Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md) for what is not there yet.

## 0. Try it without installing anything

Open the hosted preview:

```
https://kernlize.github.io/app/?preview=1
```

The preview runs the same shell UI over an offline stand-in for the `Kernl` contract, with two sample applets and no network ([D-011](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-011)). It behaves like the live shell where it stands in for it: it asks before a write only for the kinds `@kernl/core` rates destructive, using the core's own `isDestructiveKind` and `describeChange`; its guard observes and stops an applet only by quarantine; it starts in `strict` on every load; and its sample applets remove WebRTC the way kehto's prelude does. Messaging here goes nowhere; in the live shell private and legacy messages are sent for real once you sign in with an account that can encrypt ([Alpha status](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/alpha-status.md#messaging-providers-in-the-live-shell)).

**You should now see** a card headed "Who is at the keyboard?" with a **Try the preview** button. Click it, then **Open an applet**; under "Sample applets" the launcher lists *Notes* and *Pulse*, each with an **Open** button. Open *Notes*, turn on the *network* switch (it starts off, like every grant on a first run), and click **Run**. It appears in a window with buttons to try:

- **Publish a note** goes out without a prompt: a note is routine.
- **Update your profile** and **Delete a note** ask first: the consent dialog shows what changes, and nothing happens until you answer.
- **Flood the shell** sends 40 network reads at once; the guard panel (*Guard · strict · N* in the bar) records the burst.

Without `?preview=1`, `https://kernlize.github.io/app/` is the live shell: everything below from step 3 on works there too, against real relays.

## Prerequisites for running from source

- Access to the kernl source repository. It is private during the alpha; the packages are not on npm either ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)). Without access, use the hosted shell above.
- Node 22 or newer and pnpm 10. The repository pins `pnpm@10.24.0` through `packageManager`; `corepack enable` picks it up.
- A way to sign: a browser extension that speaks NIP-07, a remote signer that speaks NIP-46, or nothing, in which case the shell creates a local account protected by a password. kernl never asks for a private key directly and never stores one in plaintext.
- The address of an applet to open, which you get from the applet's publisher (an `naddr1…` or `nevent1…` string, or a coordinate). The [napplet.run app store](https://napplet.run/apps/) lists published applets; step 4 gives one you can try.

## 1. Clone, install and build

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kernlize/web.git kernl
cd kernl
pnpm install
pnpm build
```

`pnpm install` links the four workspace packages, the docs and the app. `pnpm build` compiles the packages into their `dist/` folders, which is what the app imports; skip it and the dev server cannot resolve `@kernl/…` ([Troubleshooting](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/guides/troubleshooting.md#pnpm-site-dev-before-pnpm-build)). Nothing is downloaded at runtime later; the shell's CSP would not allow it.

**You should now see** `pnpm build` finish with a `dist/` folder in each of `packages/guard`, `packages/messaging`, `packages/bridges` and `packages/core`.

## 2. Start the site

```bash
pnpm site:dev
```

This runs the Astro dev server for `apps/web`. The landing site is at the root and the shell at `/app/`:

```
http://localhost:4321/app/
```

The first load shows the shell with no account. `boot.ts` has called `createKernl({ host })`, where `host` is the page's `KernlHost`: `localStorage`, the consent dialog, the notices, link confirmation and window visibility. The guard is already running in its `strict` profile and the relay tiers are `DEFAULT_RELAY_TIERS`. Add `?preview=1` to the URL to run the offline preview instead.

**You should now see** the sign-in card, "Who is at the keyboard?", with a list headed "Sign in another way". If instead a notice says "Running the preview" with "The live shell could not start (…)", the core failed to load; see [Troubleshooting](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/guides/troubleshooting.md).

## 3. Sign in

Under "Sign in another way", pick one:

- **Use a browser extension** (button **Use**, shown only when an extension is present). The shell wraps the extension in an applesauce `ExtensionAccount`; your key stays in the extension.
- **Connect a remote signer** (button **Connect**). Either paste the code your signer app shows (a `bunker://` URI) into "Pairing code from your signer app" and click **Connect**, or click **Or pair from the signer**: the shell shows a QR code to scan with your signer app and a **Copy pairing code** button for pasting it there instead (a `nostrconnect://` URI), then waits with "Waiting for the signer to accept…". Either way the shell holds a `NostrConnectAccount` over an applesauce `NostrConnectSigner` that talks through the shell's own `RelayPool`.
- **Read-only** (button **Choose**). Paste a public key into "Account id" and click **Continue**. The session is `readOnly`: applets you grant *your account* see that public key, and every write is refused because `createAuthHooks` returns no signer.
- **Create a local account** (button **Create**). Choose a password, repeat it, and click **Create and sign in**. The shell generates a key inside an applesauce `PasswordSigner` and persists it as a `PasswordAccount`, whose serialised form is NIP-49 encrypted. A plaintext-key account is refused by `KernlAccountManager` with `denied:plaintext-key-persistence`.

Each path ends in `kernl.login(account)`, which adds the account to the `AccountManager` if it is new, makes it active and emits a `Session` on `kernl.session$`. Accounts and the active choice persist at `kernl:accounts:v1` and `kernl:active-account:v1`, so the next load lists the account under "Remembered accounts" with a **Sign in** button (a password account asks to be unlocked). Nothing is fetched at sign-in: profile, follows and relay list are loaded from the `discovery` tier the first time an applet or the shell asks for them.

```ts
import { createKernl, type KernlHost } from '@kernl/core';
import type { IAccount } from 'applesauce-accounts';

declare const host: KernlHost;
declare const account: IAccount;

const kernl = createKernl({ host, relays: { apps: ['wss://relay.napplet.soy'] } });

const session = await kernl.login(account);
session.readOnly; // true for a ReadonlyAccount; writes are then refused
```

**You should now see** the desktop: an **Open an applet** button, "Workspace 1 · 0 windows" with a button naming the current layout (`floating` or `tiled`; click it to switch), "No applets open. Press Alt + / or use the button above.", and on the right *Guard · strict · 0*, **Messages** and your account name, whose menu holds **Settings** and **Sign out**. At 720 px wide or less the bar shows **Open** and a **Menu** button instead; the menu sheet holds the guard, messages, layout, minimised windows, **Settings** and **Sign out**, and each window fills the screen.

**Settings** lists the four server tiers (Discovery, Applet catalogue, Your connections, General) by display name, so `wss://relay.damus.io` reads `damus.io`; add one by typing it into "Server address" (a bare hostname gets `wss://`). Under "Bridges" it names each bridge by what it does, *Downloads (web)*, *Downloads (from peers)*, *Downloads (archives)*, *Sharing* and *Mail*, with an "Availability" of "Ready" or "Needs a backend" and what the other side learns. "About" shows the shell's version, `kernl 0.1.0`, and whether it is live or the offline preview.

## 4. Open an applet by address

Click **Open an applet** (or press Alt+/), paste the address the applet's publisher gave you into "Applet address", and click **Look up**.

**An applet you can try.** *Freeze Frame Response*, a physics puzzle, is published by a third party in the [napplet.run](https://napplet.run/apps/) catalogue, not by kernl. It needs no grants:

```
naddr1qvzqqqyf8ypzqw49s9e88sajl985jxzquprj7pyapugqp83rme3sqctxhj5mxm4rqythwumn8ghj7un9d3shjtnwv9c8qmr9wsh8xmmeqqxkuttzvy6nyefnxpjr2e3jqg5uk8
```
 `kernl.decodePointer` accepts an `naddr1…`, an `nevent1…` or `note1…`, a bare 64-hex event id, any of those behind `nostr:`, and a coordinate in either `<pubkey>:<kind>:<identifier>` or `<kind>:<pubkey>:<identifier>` order. Anything else is `invalid:pointer`, shown as "That does not look like an applet address."

`kernl.resolve(pointer)` fetches the manifest from the pointer's relay hints plus the `apps` tier, verifies its signature, fetches the artifact bytes by hash and verifies them. Nothing runs before verification passes; a tampered artifact is `invalid:blob-hash-mismatch`, a missing one `unavailable:blob`, a manifest nobody serves `unavailable:manifest`. When it passes, the launcher shows the `AppletSummary`: title, publisher, description, and under "What it may use" the domains it `requires` and lists as `optional`, each as a switch.

Baseline domains (`shell`, `inc`, `theme`, `storage`) are marked "always on" and cannot be switched off. Every other switch starts where this identity's grants already are, which on a first run is off. That includes *your account* (`identity`): until you turn it on, the applet is not told who is signed in; a required domain is marked "the applet says it needs this", and while one is off the launcher warns "Without …, this applet may not work. You can still run it." Click **Run**. The launcher calls `kernl.grants.allowDomain` for each switch you turned on and `kernl.grants.revokeDomain` for each you turned off, then `kernl.plan(summary)`, and opens a window for the `MountPlan`. If `plan.missingRequired` is not empty, the applet sees those domains as unavailable.

<!-- sample:continues -->
```ts
declare const address: string; // from the applet's publisher

const summary = await kernl.resolve(kernl.decodePointer(address));
summary.requires; // advisory, never a grant
const plan = await kernl.plan(summary);
plan.missingRequired; // required domains the user has not allowed
```

`kernl.plan` also refuses an applet whose verified markup contains a frame element of its own, with `denied:nested-frame`, and puts kernl's frame lock in the `srcdoc` right after kehto's prelude ([D-014](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/decisions.md#d-014)). The window's iframe is mounted with `kernl.mount(plan, iframe)`: the frame gets `sandbox="allow-scripts"` and the controller-denying `allow` policy, is registered with its verified identity, has its environment frozen, is watched for a second load, and only then receives `srcdoc`. The applet sends its `hello`, which passes through the guard pipeline on its way to kehto's bridge, and `shell.init` tells it the domains it has.

**You should now see** a window titled with the applet's name, with **Grants**, **Minimise** and **Close** in its title bar. It shows "Starting …" briefly, then the applet.

## 5. Watch the guard

The desktop bar shows *Guard · strict · N*, where N counts guard events this session. Click it to see the profile, the eleven protections with the limit each one applies in the current profile (`kernl.guard.mitigations()`), and "Recent events" (`kernl.guard.events$`). Each event is a sentence naming the applet, what happened and why, for example "Applet Notes went over a limit: too many publishes", which is the guard's `rate:relay:publish`. A quarantined applet has its binding revoked and its frame removed; the window shows "This applet was stopped." and a notice says so.

Over-budget requests are refused before they are handled, by kehto's runtime firewall with the rates kernl installs at mount, and so are oversized downloads and queries; the guard panel shows kernl's count of the same budgets. Changing the profile here calls `kernl.guard.setProfile(profile)`. kernl's own counting switches at once; windows already open keep the refusal rates they were mounted with until you open them again, and the choice is not remembered across reloads. [Change the guard profile](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/change-guard-profile.md) has the details and the numbers.

**You should now see** the guard panel with `strict (default)` selected and, for a quiet applet, no events.

## 6. Grant, revoke, block

Each window's **Grants** button opens its grants panel. It lists every domain the shell offers (`kernl.grants.availableDomains()`) as a switch, with the baseline fixed on. Turning a switch on is `kernl.grants.allowDomain(identity, domain)`; off is `kernl.grants.revokeDomain(identity, domain)`. Both write kehto's ACL at once, so the applet's next call on a revoked domain is refused; the domains it was told about at mount do not change until it is opened again. Under "Standing", **Block applet** is `kernl.grants.block(identity)`: the ACL denies everything and the next mount advertises `shell` alone (**Unblock applet** reverses it). Closing the window is `handle.close()`, which revokes the binding and removes the frame; the grants stay, keyed by identity, for the next time you open the same build.

[Grant and revoke](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/grant-and-revoke.md) covers each call and what it changes.

**You should now see** the grants panel's "Standing" rows: the storage quota, "Blocked: no" and the number of guard events this window has had.

## Where next

- [Grant and revoke](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/grant-and-revoke.md) for what each prompt means and what it changes.
- [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md) if you came here to test your own applet.
- [Embed kernl core](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/embed-kernl-core.md) to run the core in your own page instead of `apps/web`.
- [Deploy](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/how-tos/deploy.md) to publish your own instance of the shell.

---

<!-- https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/write-an-applet.md -->

# Write an applet

This tutorial builds a small applet as one HTML file, checks it against the limits kernl will hold it to, publishes it with the applet format's own tooling, and opens it in kernl. The applet shows who is signed in when it is allowed to know, lists recent notes when it is allowed to read the network, and posts a note. It takes about thirty minutes, most of it in publishing.

kernl adds nothing to the applet format, so nothing here is kernl-specific except the last two steps. The authority on the format is [napplet.run](https://napplet.run/docs/), the [getting-started guide](https://napplet.run/docs/guide/getting-started.html) and the [NAP documents](https://github.com/napplet/naps). [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md) explains the posture your applet meets; this page is the hands-on version.

> **Alpha**
>
> kernl is a first draft, and so is the protocol. Step 3 needs a clone of the kernl source repository, which is private during the alpha ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)); the other steps do not.

## Prerequisites

- A text editor and a browser.
- The `napplet` CLI for publishing. Install it with `curl -fsSL https://napplet.run/install.sh | sh` (Windows: `irm https://napplet.run/install.ps1 | iex`), then check it with `napplet --version`.
- A key to sign the applet's manifest with. `napplet deploy` asks for one when it has none: a remote signer, a stored reference or a pasted secret.

## 1. Write the applet

Create a folder `hello-kernl` with one file, `index.html`:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Hello kernl</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Shows who is signed in, lists recent notes and posts one.">
  <meta name="napplet-id" content="hello-kernl">
  <meta name="napplet-optional" content="identity relay">
  <style>
    body { font: 15px/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; margin: 1.5rem; }
    li { margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello kernl</h1>
  <p id="who">Waiting for the shell…</p>
  <section id="network" hidden>
    <form id="post">
      <input id="text" placeholder="Say something" required>
      <button>Post</button>
    </form>
    <ul id="notes"></ul>
  </section>
  <p id="status" role="status"></p>
  <script type="module">
    const napplet = window.napplet;
    const status = (text) => { document.getElementById('status').textContent = text; };

    if (!napplet?.shell) {
      status('Open this page in an applet shell, such as kernl.');
    } else {
      await napplet.shell.ready();

      const who = document.getElementById('who');
      if (napplet.shell.supports('identity')) {
        const pubkey = await napplet.identity.getPublicKey();
        who.textContent = pubkey ? `Signed in as ${pubkey.slice(0, 8)}…` : 'Nobody is signed in.';
      } else {
        who.textContent = 'Allow your account to see who is signed in.';
      }

      if (napplet.shell.supports('relay')) {
        document.getElementById('network').hidden = false;
        const list = document.getElementById('notes');
        const seen = new Set();
        napplet.relay.subscribe({ kinds: [1], limit: 10 }, ({ event }) => {
          if (seen.has(event.id)) return;
          seen.add(event.id);
          const item = document.createElement('li');
          item.textContent = event.content.slice(0, 280);
          list.prepend(item);
        }, () => status('Up to date.'));

        document.getElementById('post').addEventListener('submit', async (submit) => {
          submit.preventDefault();
          const input = document.getElementById('text');
          try {
            await napplet.relay.publish({ kind: 1, content: input.value, tags: [], created_at: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) });
            input.value = '';
            status('Posted.');
          } catch (error) {
            status(`Not posted: ${error.message}`);
          }
        });
      } else {
        status('Allow network access to see and post notes.');
      }
    }
  </script>
</body>
</html>
```

What each part does:

- **The `<meta>` tags are publishing hints.** `napplet deploy` reads `description`, `napplet-id` (the applet's name in its address) and `napplet-optional`, a space-separated list of domains, from the head and signs them into the manifest. `identity` and `relay` are optional here, not required, because the applet still does something without them. A domain listed in `napplet-requires` would be marked "the applet says it needs this" in kernl's launcher. Neither grants anything: the user decides.
- **`window.napplet` is the whole API.** The shell injects it before your code runs; the applet loads no library. Outside a shell it is missing, which is why the script checks `napplet?.shell` first. `@napplet/sdk` wraps the same object in typed named exports if you prefer a bundler ([`@napplet/sdk`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@napplet/sdk)).
- **Feature detection, not assumption.** `napplet.shell.supports('relay')` is true only when the shell put `relay` on `window.napplet`, which in kernl means the user granted it. The same holds for `identity`: kernl's baseline is `shell`, `inc`, `theme` and `storage`, so an applet is not told who is signed in until the user grants "your account". Check `supports('identity')` before you read it, and say what the grant would add.
- **`shell.ready()`** waits for the shell's answer to the applet's `hello`, so the domains are settled before the applet reads them.
- **Routine writes only.** A kind 1 note is routine, so kernl signs it without a prompt. If your applet updated the user's profile (kind 0) or deleted something (kind 5), kernl would show the user what changes and wait; a refusal arrives as an error that names `denied:consent`.
- **Errors are shown, not thrown away.** A publish over the shell's budget is refused with an error that starts `firewall:`; the applet prints it.
- **No frames, no Trusted Types policy of its own.** The list is built with `createElement` and `textContent`. kernl refuses to mount markup that contains an `iframe`, `object`, `embed` or other frame element, makes every attempt to create one throw `denied:nested-frame`, and reserves the Trusted Types `default` policy for that lock, so an applet must not create a frame or register a Trusted Types policy ([Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md#what-the-strict-profile-means-for-you)).

The file has no network access of its own and needs none: inline script and style are allowed, and everything else goes through the shell ([No network path](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#no-network-path)).

**Checkpoint.** Open `index.html` directly in a browser. You should see "Hello kernl" and "Open this page in an applet shell, such as kernl." Nothing else happens, because there is no shell.

## 2. Know the limits it will meet

Under kernl's `strict` profile, which every load starts in, the limits that matter for this applet are:

| What the applet does | Limit in `strict` | What happens past it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Posts notes (`relay.publish`) | 20 per 60 s per applet | kehto's runtime firewall refuses the publish; the applet sees an error starting `firewall:` |
| Reads the network (`relay.subscribe`) | 30 per 60 s | refused the same way |
| Sends messages to the shell in its first 3 s | 20 | kehto's runtime firewall refuses the rest of the burst with a `firewall:` error |
| Sends messages to the shell at all | 8 per second | reported to the user as a burst, still handled |
| Sends messages to the shell at all | 300 in any 10 s | the applet is quarantined: the message that crossed the limit is dropped and the applet is closed |
| Downloads while hidden (`resource.*`) | 8 | the ninth quarantines the applet |
| Asks for a download or a query larger than the cap | 64 KiB for `resource.*`, 256 KiB for subscriptions and queries | refused before it is handled, with a `firewall:` error |

This applet sends a handful of messages at start-up, opens one subscription and publishes once per click, so it stays far inside every limit. The full list is in [Guard](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/guard.md#profiles).

## 3. Test it against the guard

kernl's guard is a pure package, so you can replay your applet's traffic through it in a test, without a browser, and see which events the user would see. This needs the kernl source ([Packages](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/packages/index.md#install)). The function below feeds the guard each message the way the shell does: the ingress guard counts it first, and the focus firewall measures it unless it was held or quarantined.

```ts
import { createFocusFirewall, createGuardConfig, createIngressGuard, type GuardEnvelope, type GuardEvent } from '@kernl/guard';

const events: GuardEvent[] = [];
let clock = 0;
const config = createGuardConfig('strict');
const options = { config, now: () => clock, onEvent: (event: GuardEvent) => events.push(event) };
const ingress = createIngressGuard(options);
const firewall = createFocusFirewall(options);

function send(envelope: GuardEnvelope, visibility = { visible: true, focused: true }): string {
  const disposition = ingress.admit('w1', 'hello-kernl', envelope, visibility);
  if (disposition === 'pass') firewall.observe('w1', 'hello-kernl', envelope, visibility);
  return disposition;
}

// Start-up: the readiness signal, the identity read and the one subscription.
send({ type: 'shell.ready' });
send({ type: 'identity.getPublicKey' });
send({ type: 'relay.subscribe', size: 120 });

// A user, or a bug, that posts once a second for a minute.
const firstReport: number[] = [];
for (let post = 1; post <= 60; post += 1) {
  clock += 1000;
  const before = events.length;
  send({ type: 'relay.publish', kind: 1, size: 300 });
  if (events.length > before) firstReport.push(post);
}

const reasons = new Set(events.map((event) => event.reason));
// Start-up is quiet. From about the 30th post on, the posts outrun the
// 20-per-minute budget: `reasons` is { 'rate:relay:publish' } and `firstReport[0]`
// is near 30. In the shell, kehto's runtime firewall, which kernl configures
// with the same rates, refuses those posts.
```

Change the loop to model your own applet: a burst of subscriptions on start-up, a hidden window (`send(envelope, { visible: false, focused: false })`) or a background poll. What `events` holds is what the guard panel would show the user. [Applets under kernl](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/concepts/applets-under-kernl.md#test-against-the-guard) adds the visibility gate and lists scenarios worth writing.

To see the applet run inside a real shell runtime on your machine, the napplet CLI can serve it in kehto's Paja preview (`napplet paja`, see the [CLI reference](https://napplet.run/docs/)). Paja runs the same kehto runtime kernl composes, without kernl's opinions: it is a quick way to check the applet's behaviour, not kernl's guard.

## 4. Publish it

Publishing signs a manifest that names your file by its hash, uploads the file to a Blossom server and announces the manifest on relays. kernl verifies the hash before anything runs, so the bytes it runs are exactly the bytes you published.

From the `hello-kernl` folder:

```bash
napplet init --source-dir . --name hello-kernl --title "Hello kernl" --relay wss://relay.napplet.soy --server https://blossom.example
napplet deploy --dry-run
napplet deploy
```

Replace `https://blossom.example` with a Blossom server you can upload to; `napplet init` without flags suggests some. `wss://relay.napplet.soy` is the relay in kernl's applet catalogue tier by default, so kernl finds the manifest there without extra settings. `napplet deploy --dry-run` shows the plan and the signed manifest without uploading anything; `napplet deploy` does the upload and prints the applet's address, an `naddr1…` string. Copy it.

If you build with Vite instead of writing one file by hand, `@napplet/vite-plugin` inlines your code into a single `index.html` and writes the same manifest fields from its options (`nappletType`, `requires`, `optional`); `napplet create` starts such a project. The [napplet.run docs](https://napplet.run/docs/) cover both paths.

**Checkpoint.** `napplet deploy` reports the upload and the publish as complete and prints an `naddr1…` address.

## 5. Open it in kernl

Open the shell, either the hosted one at `https://kernlize.github.io/app/` or your own from [Run the shell](https://kernlize.github.io/docs/tutorials/run-the-shell.md), and sign in. The offline preview (`?preview=1`) cannot open your applet: it has no network and runs only its two sample applets.

1. Click **Open an applet**, paste the address into "Applet address" and click **Look up**. kernl fetches the manifest, verifies its signature, fetches your file by hash and verifies it.
2. The launcher shows the title, publisher and description, and under "What it may use" switches for *your account* and *network*, each marked "optional" and off. Click **Run** with both off first.
3. The window shows "Allow your account to see who is signed in." and "Allow network access to see and post notes." That is your feature detection at work.
4. Click the window's **Grants** button and turn *your account* and *network* on. The grant applies to the running window's next request, but the domains an applet was told about at start-up do not change until it is opened again, so close the window and open the applet again from "Recent" in the launcher.
5. Now the window shows "Signed in as …", the notes appear, and **Post** works without a prompt.

If you published to a relay that is not in kernl's catalogue tier and the address carries no relay hint, the lookup finds nothing: add the relay under **Settings**, "Applet catalogue", "Server address", and try again.

**You should now see** your applet in a window titled "Hello kernl", and *Guard · strict · 0* in the bar: a well-behaved applet triggers no guard events. Click it to see the protections and, if you push the applet past a limit, the events it caused, each naming your applet.
